item.description: After defining its internal software factory entirely as code and wiring in an observability loop, Warp compressed PR costs from $80 to $15–20 through measure-and-optimize, while lifting PR throughput 40%.
item.content:encoded:
After defining its internal software factory entirely as code and wiring in an observability loop, Warp compressed PR costs from $80 to $15–20 through measure-and-optimize, while lifting PR throughput 40%.

Breaks down the layered technical stack a software factory needs, shows Warp's before/after real costs and throughput when tuning its agent system—numbers a team can benchmark against, not product talk.

2:03 Software factories aren't built by bolting automation together
Zach argues that most companies calling themselves a software factory have simply added some agent-assisted coding—a fundamental misunderstanding. His definition: a cloud-hosted agentic system where teams explicitly define agent roles in the build process, the system exercises autonomy, is measurable and benchmarkable, forms a closed loop, and can be tuned over time to build confidence. That's categorically different from ad-hoc automation.

4:10 The factory definition itself must run as code
Against the myth that "buy a tool and get a money machine," Zach insists the factory must be concrete and runnable. Define it in YAML: which repos, which MCP integrations, which skills. Write the entire workflow declaratively—like Terraform—so it versions, branches for testing, and rolls back on demand. That's the only way to escape loose automation fragments that can't be versioned or audited.

6:15 All agent work, wherever it starts, must feed one central system
Whether a task lands in Slack, Linear, or GitHub, it must enter the same system to trigger pre-defined workflows. Only then do you see the complete trace: computer-use screenshots, every orchestration detail, agent-to-agent handoffs. Most companies can't do this because engineers each run Cloud Code or Codex locally, data completely fragmented across laptops and logs.

14:36 Agents should submit pull requests to improve the factory code
Because the factory definition is code, Warp's self-improving agents analyze historical failures—they spotted 54 cases where the triage agent should have spawned sub-agents but didn't—then submit PRs directly to the factory definition to fix the workflow. It's a complete learning loop, though Zach admits they haven't yet replayed history to verify the fix actually works. That's the next-level capability being built now.

16:41 Real benchmarks must test model and harness combinations together
Zach argues you can't benchmark models in isolation; you must benchmark models and harness together. Warp runs the same real-world tasks with different model/harness combinations (Warp's own, Cloud Code, Codex, Pi), plots cost-versus-correctness curves, gets results for their specific business rather than generic leaderboards, then feeds those results into model/harness routing strategy.

23:51 Tuning can cut per-PR costs to one-quarter of starting point
Warp tuned its own system this way: started at ~$80 per PR (too much Opus, over-trained triage models, sub-agents split too finely); brought it down to $15–20. Month-over-month, PR throughput jumped 40% while revert rate stayed flat. Zach calls that the proof that observe-measure-optimize actually works—not just in theory but in the production cost structure of an agentic platform.

26:58 Teams smaller than five to ten engineers should not use this
Asked who really needs this platform, Zach draws a clear line: small teams just buy Cloud Code or Codex; this platform is overkill for them. The real breakeven is roughly 5–10 engineers and up. Bigger companies need it more, but deployment complexity grows with scale. Growth-stage companies at 10–100 people with Slack and Linear already in place can often self-serve.

31:07 When API costs are too high, small companies rotate subscriptions
On the hardest objection: some small companies desperately want this system but can't afford it, so they're cycling through $200 subscriptions to piece together capacity, because per-API billing runs 5–50 times more expensive than subscriptions. Zach admits he's unsure whether rotating subscriptions violates the service terms, but concedes it's currently the cheapest way—it just doesn't scale as a company grows.

item.title: Anthropic's bill makes it nearly impossible to halt dangerous AI training
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-03-eightythousand-anthropic的法案让人几乎没法叫停危险的ai训练/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-03-eightythousand-anthropic的法案让人几乎没法叫停危险的ai训练/
item.description: The bill compresses the power to halt training into a single Commerce Secretary signature and a single DC court decision within 45 days—when models actually cause harm, there's almost no time to hit the brakes.
item.content:encoded:
The bill compresses the power to halt training into a single Commerce Secretary signature and a single DC court decision within 45 days—when models actually cause harm, there's almost no time to hit the brakes.

A dense solo episode: the evidence chains and perspectives on three major scandals are laid out clearly and worth hearing in full.

1:34 Bill compresses authority to stop dangerous training through a dangerously narrow bottleneck
Under the federal AI bill that Anthropic privately championed, the only way to halt a model's training is for the Commerce Secretary to personally sign off and submit the case to a single federal court in Washington DC. The government must prove the risk is ‘imminent’, must prove lighter interventions won't work, and judges must review from scratch without deference to regulators. Any halt order expires automatically after 45 days; reauthorizing requires proving the case all over again. More critically, even whether ‘a 10% human extinction probability within the next year’counts as ‘imminent’ is undefined—and that gap determines whether this gate can actually block truly catastrophic risks.

4:02 CEO estimates 25% disaster probability, yet company strips halt authority
The contradiction: this bill comes from a company whose CEO publicly puts the probability of AI ‘causing major chaos’at 25% and has written that ‘recursive self-improvement must proceed with extreme care, if at all’. The host sees why—Anthropic has been in frequent conflict with the Trump administration this year and fears federal discretionary power will be weaponized for political concessions rather than genuinely controlling dangerous research. But he argues the solution shouldn't be stripping away state power too; instead preserve states like California's independent halt authority, or at least let state attorneys general petition the DC court as well. You shouldn't stake everything on one agency's review by a single court.

5:15 Bill would retroactively eliminate state-level AI safety laws nationwide
The bill not only narrows federal authority but also bars states from requiring AI companies to disclose safety plans, undergo independent audits, or report incidents—effectively retroactively nullifying flagship AI laws already passed in California, Illinois, and New York. There's a subtler provision: states had the power to halt models presenting ‘major catastrophic risk’using ‘statute, regulation, directive, court decision or other action’; under the bill's design, that power eventually disappears too. The result: even if California's government unanimously determined an unreleased model could kill everyone in the state, it would have no power to legislate or seek a court injunction—only hope the Commerce Secretary will run that process.

8:58 OpenAI fired three safety researchers on the same afternoon over disputed evidence
Tomek Korbak, Mikita Balesni, and Jasmine Wang were each fired at a 2 p.m. meeting on the same afternoon, with contradictory and unpersuasive justifications. OpenAI later claimed the real reason was ‘broken trust’but refused to explain. According to reports, the trigger was a leak investigation: news had surfaced that OpenAI's new model used ‘looped transformer’technology, which the company wanted hidden. Investigators suspected the leak came via Signal messages between one researcher and outside contact Ryan Greenblatt, but both used disappearing messages—neither could prove innocence. Looped transformers let models perform hidden calculations before outputting chain-of-thought reasoning; the field has long warned this points toward unmonitorable models. All three researchers had previously publicly supported keeping chain-of-thought observable.

10:12 The evidence for firing the three was far weaker than stated
Disappearing messages are standard in tech and AI circles—you can't convict based on that alone, or everyone from CEO down would be suspect. The Information, which broke this story, has sourced OpenAI's internal secrets for years from investors, ex-employees, even casual conversation—not necessarily these three. Hundreds, possibly two hundred OpenAI employees could oppose looped transformers—this year alone, nearly 400 signed a petition demanding AI research slow for safety's sake. The host personally judges a Greenblatt leak highly unlikely; it doesn't fit his operating style at all. Conclusion: firing was probably error. The cost: the company will struggle to get candid employee input going forward, and the actual leaker may never be found.

12:52 Google DeepMind's contracts silence employees for life, not just at departure
According to BBC reporting, Google DeepMind's UK employment contracts forbid employees from publicly criticizing anything Google does—for life. The clause surfaced when a former employee tried to criticize Google's sale of AI to the US Defense Department (usable as long as DoD deems it legal), a deal that already prompted resignations over principle. This echoes the ‘non-disparagement agreement’scandal uncovered two years ago at OpenAI: former employees criticizing the company lost stock worth potentially tens of millions, and the clause itself demanded secrecy. After exposure, both OpenAI and Anthropic admitted to similar clauses and promised to drop them. Google DeepMind's version has no secrecy requirement and doesn't forfeit stock, but the lawsuit threat alone creates massive chilling effect on ordinary employees.

17:31 Speaking up inside requires public channels; speaking out requires going public
The host offers a graduated approach: to stay, calmly and rationally explain specific reasons for opposing a decision in public Slack channels colleagues will see, focusing on the few most critical points, not opposing everything reflexively, and staying open to being persuaded. If reasonable dissent gets no satisfactory response, escalate to publicly stating this makes you question the company's judgment and strategy—and that you're considering leaving. Still no results: submit a thorough resignation statement, then make your case public after departure. His reasoning: companies automate employee work faster by the year, so employees' bargaining power erodes over time. ‘If not now, when?’

21:39 Outside pressure reshapes corporate governance when insiders organize the pressure
Against OpenAI's plan to hollow out its nonprofit parent and charitable mission, the ‘Not For Private Gain’campaign had few participants but, paired with state attorneys general attention and broader coalition pressure, forced OpenAI to substantially revise: the OpenAI Foundation gained approximately 75 billion dollars in additional equity, and its Safety & Alignment Committee locked down decision rights over a range of safety questions. Similar: a 2024 campaign by former employees for ‘right to raise concerns’that became whistleblower protections in California's SB 53; continued reporting showing OpenAI publicly backing regulation while lobbying against it also pushed OpenAI to support SB 53-type rules and led President Greg Brockman to stop giving to the lobbying PAC ‘Leading the Future’.

item.title: Your A-share losses come from understanding that can't keep pace with change
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-03-touzishizhan-亏钱不是a股的错-是你对它的认知不够/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-03-touzishizhan-亏钱不是a股的错-是你对它的认知不够/
item.description: After reviewing his 60+-percent drawdown this year, Zhang Jun discovered that the root cause of A-shares' short bull runs and long bear markets—and investors' short time horizons—was never the market itself, but investors' understanding of intrinsic value and macroeconomic cycles failing to keep pace with change's speed.
item.content:encoded:
After reviewing his 60+-percent drawdown this year, Zhang Jun discovered that the root cause of A-shares' short bull runs and long bear markets—and investors' short time horizons—was never the market itself, but investors' understanding of intrinsic value and macroeconomic cycles failing to keep pace with change's speed.

An honest retrospective from a fund manager running private equity for years after a major drawdown, from rereading Graham's original work to the storage-chip case—information-dense.

4:09 The index barely moved, but whole sectors were sliced in half
Zhang Jun highlights a counterintuitive fact: Shanghai Composite's full-year range was under 20 percent, from January highs above 4,200 to lows above 3,600. Yet beneath that, sub-indices swung wildly. ChiNext and STAR Board each fell roughly 40 percent from June peaks; the optical module index dropped over 50 percent from its high. His point: concentrated sector bets faced far steeper drawdowns than the aggregate index suggests.

5:09 Even dividend low-volatility funds got turned into high-volatility assets
Zhang Jun adds that supposedly defensive dividend plays didn't escape the carnage: the baijiu index fell 30-odd percent on its worst days; the dividend low-volatility index—promised stability—was down 10 points in its worst month. More tragicomically, in June when the market rallied and tech soared, this index fell 10 points in a single month, then gained them back in July when the market fell—behaving the exact opposite of its name.

12:12 Every industry has its own Xu Jiayin
Zhang Jun argues Chinese firms cannot sustain stable EPS growth because of abundant ‘entrepreneurial ambition’: CEOs want to expand scale, CFOs and key technologists push expansion and capex to advance their careers, and local governments' investment drives force companies to boost capital spending. Everyone knows Xu Jiayin, he notes, but every industry has its own version—the property sector's just leveraged hard enough to crater publicly.

20:14 Graham never said to discount future cash flows
Zhang Jun revisits years of misreading Graham: value investors picture DCF models calculating intrinsic value, but that was Williams' idea, not Graham's. In “Security Analysis”, Graham calculated working capital and net asset discounts—the goal was finding a margin of safety, not pinning an exact intrinsic value number. He restates Graham's actual logic in three sentences: stocks are stakes in businesses; Mr. Market is a quotation device to exploit; and margins of safety matter.

22:15 Intrinsic value isn't a point—it's a moving range
He cites a cutting-tool stock he sold too early this year: bought at 2 billion+ market cap aiming for 10 billion in three years, but AI-driven M&A turbocharged earnings to target, so he sold per plan—only later discovering the company's intrinsic value was still climbing fast and he'd treated a dynamic company as static. Takeaway: intrinsic value is never a fixed point but a range that shifts up and down with fundamentals; exit timing should track that range's velocity.

31:22 Storage chip prices spike, but intrinsic value may not follow
When asked whether ‘rising demand equals rising intrinsic value,’ Zhang Jun uses storage chips to refute the simple narrative: Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron learned overexpansion's sting, intentionally restrained supply to barely maintain a three-player oligopoly—then AI sent prices skyward, but now they're expanding again while YMTC enters. His conclusion: once a carefully guarded competitive structure cracks, surface price rallies and demand figures don't simply equal long-term intrinsic-value gains.

35:25 Whether to add on dips—the question itself is the answer
Facing scenarios where stock price falls below your entry but intrinsic value falls faster (so margin of safety looks bigger), Zhang Jun offers this heuristic: if you're asking friends whether to add to a losing position, that act alone proves you don't understand it well enough—sell immediately. As long as intrinsic value is still sliding and you can't find new evidence of a bottom, buying purely because the price is low is short-term gambling and probably catching a knife mid-fall.

50:42 Value investors with sweeping sector coverage—I'm skeptical
Zhang Jun offers an ‘immature observation’: no one can be expert in packaged food, consumer electronics, and AI simultaneously. If someone calling themselves a value investor covers too many industries, he doubts their authenticity. He reviews his own past expansion into chemicals, pharma, information security, and solar—convinced at the time he was applying value-investing method, but in hindsight nearly every call was wrong. Example: pharma volume-based pricing policy disruptions happened long before he grasped that industry logic had shifted.

item.title: Next fiscal year, Nvidia must finance a quarter of its own revenue
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-03-laoshi-下一财年-英伟达四分之一营收要靠自己给客户撑腰/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-03-laoshi-下一财年-英伟达四分之一营收要靠自己给客户撑腰/
item.description: Nvidia packages GPUs as financeable assets while funding AI labs and extending credit to customers buying its chips, propping up revenue through circular financing and driving accounts receivable to $63.1 billion.
item.content:encoded:
Nvidia packages GPUs as financeable assets while funding AI labs and extending credit to customers buying its chips, propping up revenue through circular financing and driving accounts receivable to $63.1 billion.

Complete breakdown of Nvidia's production, capital, and industrial strategy at three levels; circular financing and accounts receivable are most valuable for assessing whether AI infrastructure is overheating.

1:02 Computing power is revenue—Jevons Paradox means cheaper chips drive volume growth
Huang has inverted the old accounting. GPUs were once an expense to minimize; now they're production assets that generate returns. But his wager rests on Jevons Paradox: as compute gets cheaper, the surge in demand activates new use cases—contract reviews, email, simulation—that were economically unviable before. Volume must grow fast enough to offset falling prices. If it does, Nvidia widens margins despite cheaper chips.

4:02 AI agents never sleep—they parallelize and multiply compute demand by orders of magnitude
Agents differ from humans: they reason, plan, call tools, iterate repeatedly, work without sleeping or procrastinating, and can spawn hundreds of copies running in parallel. An engineer might manually run dozens of simulations a day; an agent can generate thousands of parameter combinations and optimize them autonomously. Human software interactions are dropping while background compute demand explodes. Agents don't just need GPU—they need CPU for scheduling, memory and storage for state, networking to connect tools and systems. One machine's gains lift everything around it.

5:03 Tokens are intermediate products; value is solving problems correctly, not token count
A steel mill produces a ton of steel, sells it, makes cash. An AI factory produces ten million tokens that might be worth nothing. An agent might spin for an hour burning millions of tokens to fix a bug, only to make the code worse, forcing engineers to spend extra time cleaning up the mess. Nvidia cares about tokens-per-watt and tokens-per-dollar. Users care about spending money to solve one thing correctly. When they align, everyone wins. When algorithm innovation lets models use fewer tokens for the same task, that's good for users—but not necessarily for vendors selling hardware by token throughput.

7:03 Per gigawatt, Nvidia captures revenue from $18 billion to $40 billion across chip generations
The AI factory's total efficiency—not a single GPU—determines pricing power. By Nvidia's own math, for each gigawatt of power a customer receives, the device-purchase revenue flowing to Nvidia was approximately $18 billion in the Hopper era, $25 billion in Blackwell, and $40 billion in the Vera Rubin generation. That extra money isn't higher GPU prices. It's that Nvidia has more to sell: networking, software, the full stack ecosystem. Even if customers use competitors' GPUs or custom silicon, networking and systems still flow through Nvidia. It keeps collecting rent.

8:03 DSXPORT cuts data center deployment from six months to as little as two weeks
DSXPORT pre-assembles entire AI factories in modular containers—racks, wiring, liquid cooling, system validation—all done in the factory. At the site, power, cooling, and networking just need to be ready. Deployment time drops from six months to as little as fourteen days. Huang's calculation: an AI factory generates $40 billion annually in revenue; three months of delay is tens of billions in sunk loss. But gross margins on infrastructure components don't match GPU margins, and this quarter's 75% overall gross margin may face seasonal pressure ahead.

13:08 Circular financing inflates revenue while extending credit disguised as long payment terms
Nvidia's management keeps repeating three words—productive, fungible, durable—to convince Wall Street that GPUs are stable, long-term, resellable assets. Customers can then use equipment as loan collateral. Nvidia itself invests heavily: supply and capacity commitments now exceed $279 billion, plus nearly $50 billion into AI labs. This quarter's $96.2 billion revenue grew 106% year-over-year. Yet accounts receivable hit $63.1 billion with collection periods around sixty days. More revenue isn't real cash. It's extended as long payment terms, accounting entries sitting with customers. Nvidia is using its own balance sheet to funnel hidden loans.

17:10 Every AI strategy—U.S., China, Europe—must pay Nvidia's infrastructure toll regardless of approach
The U.S. pursues frontier models plus high-value services; the challenge is whether billion-dollar investments pay back and custom chips reduce Nvidia reliance. China pursues open ecosystems and extreme engineering efficiency; DeepSeek and other open models lower the barrier to entry, paired with manufacturing-sector AI deployment; the challenge is competing under compute constraints. Europe pursues industrial applications and sovereign AI—adapting open models to local industrial data for domain-specific training. The earnings report signals the outcome: ACIE customers (non-hyperscaler data centers) contributed roughly $40 billion, up 138% year-over-year, outpacing overall data-center growth. Every path requires paying Nvidia's toll.

19:14 Nvidia's model survives only if three conditions hold: productivity gains, capital access, market share
Three balance sheets determine how long Huang's economics last. The technology account asks: does AI actually raise productivity, or does it stop at keynote demos? The capital account asks: is AI infrastructure expansion funded by customer subscriptions or increasingly by Wall Street financing and Nvidia's own balance sheet propping it up? Circular financing that re-invests its own returns is a snowball that eventually needs an accounting. The industry account asks: after markets mature, will open models and application companies capture a larger slice? Huang's historical reminder: the biggest winner in a technological revolution isn't always whoever solved the infrastructure bottleneck first.

item.title: Large models are manufacturing, not magic: no lead lasts more than a month
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-03-chinatalk-大模型是制造业不是魔法-谁都别想领先超过一个月/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-03-chinatalk-大模型是制造业不是魔法-谁都别想领先超过一个月/
item.description: The author of Death Knell for AI argues that large model makers have no protectable technical differences—data and compute are production inputs, just like in solar, phones, and EVs. No lead lasts more than a month.
item.content:encoded:
The author of Death Knell for AI argues that large model makers have no protectable technical differences—data and compute are production inputs, just like in solar, phones, and EVs. No lead lasts more than a month.

Information density is uneven: the first half is a humorist's monologue, but the second half packs a specific mechanism or data point every ten minutes that could reshape how you think about China's AI industry.

6:25 AI skills follow a seesaw: better coding, weaker prose
Xian Yu stopped using AI for writing in mid-2025—he finds it more satisfying to write himself, and the model simply can't translate original thought into personal voice. Language models can replace programmers but can't capture how a person thinks. The reason is a tradeoff in training: vendors pour resources into agentic programming datasets at the expense of writing datasets—‘it's like a whack-a-mole game’. By September 2026, coding ability kept improving while creative writing and the ability to express human thought fell, and noticeably so.

14:38 College students paid $10 to find the real ranking
In the past six months, ByteDance's Seedance series dominated video models globally. Xian Yu and his partner wanted a more interesting way to evaluate models than tech benchmarks, so they built wild prompts from memes popular on Bilibili and TikTok, had different models generate videos, then hired college students (about 300 of them) to rate the results for 10 yuan each. When H3, which MiniMax had just open-sourced, outranked Seedance 2.0 and 2.5 in their meme test—contradicting the narrative that ‘Seedance is comprehensively dominant’—Xian Yu seriously considered using technical methods to suppress H3's ranking but ultimately didn't. He thinks H3 won because it was optimized for tasks ordinary users care about (image-to-video, effects), while Seedance targets professional film studios.

23:53 When competitors complain, read it as insecurity
In July, Xian Yu published an article saying MiniMax's base model M3 had fallen behind competitors like Qwen and GLM because it hadn't been updated in four or five months. MiniMax, sensitive to ‘lagging behind’ getting out (it's public, stock price matters), filed a complaint. Xian Yu rewrote the piece as satire: ‘MiniMax is advancing so fast, we apologize to MiniMax’. Coincidentally, the day the apology went live, MiniMax's recruiter added his partner on WeChat asking about joining. This told Xian Yu the complaint was personal, not the company's official stance. Later MiniMax invited his partner to discuss technology—the relationship improved, and Xian Yu wore a MiniMax shirt to record this episode.

28:57 China's AI narrative cycles every three months, copying Silicon Valley
Chinese AI startups rotate through themes on a three-month cycle, entirely following Silicon Valley's rhythm: whatever the Valley embraces, someone in China builds a clone project to raise money. After Manus popularized the autonomous agent narrative in early 2025, waves of people entered AI applications, but most lacked real user insight—pure self-serving entrepreneurship. The ‘users build agents’narrative had a moment too, but those products mostly died because product building is far harder than TikTok clips; ordinary users can't participate. By early this year, the torch passed to ‘world models’—all because Li Feifei and others are working on them, so dollar-based VCs want domestic copy-cats.

36:08 Most ‘world models’projects are repackaged video models
Xian Yu thinks the world model wave is largely storytelling: you know if an AI app works in one or two months, and if it doesn't retain users, it dies. But world models take three years to validate, and demos don't really matter—people are buying the narrative and upside. Most domestic ‘world models’projects take Alibaba's open-source video model One from a year ago, fine-tune it into digital humans or real-time generation, and wrap it in grander language. Hype has already cooled in the past few months, but after MiniMax open-sourced H3, these storytelling projects came back alive—H3 digital humans look much better than One, so they can show new demos and keep pitching.

42:21 China's AI industry doesn't invent terms because it lacks confidence
There's an obvious pattern: Chinese AI barely invents terminology—the trendiest terms like RSI (recursive self-improvement) are all American. Company names are mostly English too (DeepSeek, MiniMax). It's not a technology problem, Xian Yu says; it's a confidence problem. The logic is ‘whatever Silicon Valley does, we build a replacement’, and funding sources matter: dollar-based LPs prefer the story of ‘cloning hot Valley trends, but cheaper and more efficient’. He points out that when investors see the same benchmark, they nearly always believe it if you tell them OpenAI did it over a Chinese company doing it. But he admits inventing terms isn't always good—the domestic model leap forward over the past few months might exist precisely because people were heads-down shipping, not debating grand concepts.

49:29 Large models follow manufacturing logic: no technical secrets survive
Xian Yu sees the large model business as fundamentally manufacturing, with no truly proprietary technical secrets. How to build datasets and scale is a small circle—model makers hire from each other constantly, so there are no secrets. Compute isn't a secret either; anyone can stack cards. Give a model more data and compute (production inputs) and you get a stronger model. This chain needs no breakthrough innovation, just engineering to push scaling laws. It's the same logic as solar panels, phones, and electric cars—you can't name fundamental technical differences between EV makers, yet market share still shifts. Competition is brutal: any model's lead rarely lasts two months, usually just one. China's GLM 5.3, Qwen 3.8 Max, and K3 all ship within a month, landing in the same ability band.

1:01:43 More money flowing in, crazier the people get
Xian Yu wraps up by noting that most people he knows are normal—just a bit unusual personality-wise. But AI is flooded with ‘so many liars, narcissists (NPD), and people doing who-knows-what’, and these people actually raise money and become industry stars. Half-joking, he suggests someone should study mental-health metrics in AI: rates of NPD or ADHD probably skew absurdly high. By contrast, ordinary AI app founders raise money at valuations under a few tens of millions of dollars; for model makers, Kimi's latest round values it at $5 billion. His conclusion: the industry has taken in so much hot money, yet the people are so odd—hot money and oddness are probably positively correlated.

item.title: America's nuclear fuel cutoff countdown: must build domestic uranium enrichment by 2028
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-03-cheekypint-美国核燃料断供倒计时-2028年前必须自己造出浓缩铀/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-03-cheekypint-美国核燃料断供倒计时-2028年前必须自己造出浓缩铀/
item.description: After the Cold War, America abandoned its uranium enrichment capacity and turned to importing Russian nuclear fuel; Congress set a 2028 ban, and General Matter must build domestic capacity by then.
item.content:encoded:
After the Cold War, America abandoned its uranium enrichment capacity and turned to importing Russian nuclear fuel; Congress set a 2028 ban, and General Matter must build domestic capacity by then.

The founder explains the five-step uranium enrichment process, why nuclear power became expensive, and how to tackle a capacity project with a hard deadline using SpaceX-style pace.

1:03 The hardest part isn't the license, it's the fuel
Venture capitalist Scott Nolan spent a decade assuming new nuclear companies' biggest hurdle was getting NRC approval—until he asked them what was really hard and got an unexpected answer: fuel. America's 94 reactors generate 20% of its electricity, yet whether new or established, every company must import enriched uranium from Russia or Europe. The U.S. has no domestic commercial supplier. Congress has already passed legislation: effective January 1, 2028, Russian uranium imports are banned.

9:22 Smaller reactors require higher-enrichment uranium fuel
To make small modular reactors (SMRs) compact enough for factory production, fuel enrichment must jump from today's 3-5% to nearly 20%—HALEU. Lower enrichment requires larger cores to maintain criticality; higher enrichment allows smaller cores and stretches refueling intervals from 18-24 months to 5-10 years. This matters most for reactors deployed in remote locations.

12:13 The AI boom hasn't yet driven nuclear power adoption
Though everyone talks about AI data centers spinning up with natural gas turbines, Scott Nolan says it barely affects their business. For the next few years, the real contracts come from utilities running those 94 existing grid reactors—even if data centers run on gas for now. The real inflection comes later, when baseload demand shifts to ‘safe, clean, reliable’. That's when it matters whether gigawatt-scale reactors or SMRs fill the gap.

15:27 Nuclear didn't get expensive because of Three Mile Island
Conventional wisdom blames Three Mile Island and Chernobyl for stopping nuclear. Nolan says safety concerns only accelerated the decline—the real culprit is that nuclear never achieved economies of scale. Each plant built itself, supply chains never formed, workers migrated between projects. Vogtle's cost overruns are brutal. Interest rates were at historic lows, yet 20% of the overrun came from interest costs. Over a decade build time, interest rates and schedule matter more than spot construction costs.

17:56 Power utilities use cost-plus contracts; no one wants to cut prices
There's an incentive layer too. Utilities mostly operate on cost-plus contracts, outsourcing plant construction, so no one in the ecosystem has real pressure to cut costs. Nolan compares this to old-school space launch: without genuine market competition, everyone collects rent in their corner instead of racing on price.

32:27 Fuel costs can represent half of an SMR's total expense
Nolan uses SpaceX as a parallel: when satellites cost $1 billion, a $100 million launch was a small fraction. But smaller, cheaper satellites? Launch becomes the lever. Same with SMRs. The plant shrinks from a $10-billion megaproject, yet fuel costs rise as a fraction—fuel costs can hit 50% of levelized cost in some SMRs. It's the largest lever General Matter believes it can move.

44:11 Uranium enrichment technology hasn't been redesigned in fifty years
Cost advantage, Nolan says, comes from three sources: scale, simplified processes, and the one most overlooked—dormant technical progress. Globally, Russia, China, and two European companies all use the same underlying enrichment technology. Since the 1950s-60s, no one has redesigned it from scratch. Fifty years of technical improvements have never been applied to enrichment. That's the gap new entrants can exploit.

53:19 Avoid competition first, then talk about scale
Reflecting on Founders Fund's investment philosophy, Nolan says the move is not to charge a trillion-dollar market on day one, but to find a small market with genuine need for a new solution, lock in those customers until they depend on you, then expand. Startup thresholds should be extreme: the mission must be critical, no one else is doing it, and it matches your capabilities. That intersection is tiny—which is why SpaceX, Anduril, and General Matter each emerged about a decade apart.

item.title: Founders have only two peak focus windows daily; interruptions cost exponentially
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-03-a16z-创始人每天只有两段黄金专注期-被打断代价是指数级的/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-03-a16z-创始人每天只有两段黄金专注期-被打断代价是指数级的/
item.description: Huberman says most people have only two or three truly productive focus windows per day; when that time is interrupted by unrelated matters, the loss isn't just those hours—it compounds exponentially against total output.
item.content:encoded:
Huberman says most people have only two or three truly productive focus windows per day; when that time is interrupted by unrelated matters, the loss isn't just those hours—it compounds exponentially against total output.

You get his complete daily schedule from wake to sleep, specific training protocols, and precise supplement dosing—dense information for anyone seeking a ready-made template. The casual conversation and self-deprecation can be skipped.

7:15 On workout days, take caffeine immediately after light exposure, not a half-hour later
When scheduling a workout, Huberman drinks caffeine-containing yerba mate immediately after sun exposure—not waiting even a minute, rather than following a fixed timetable. This means he ties caffeine intake to whether he's exercising that day, not his wake time. On rest days, he postpones caffeine later.

8:15 Staying injury-free for 35 years meant never chasing others' training routines
Huberman credits his health at 50 not to mastering specific training methods but to a 35-year discipline: never switching to another person's routine on impulse just because they challenged him to try it—the easiest path to injury. He does only movements his body feels good doing, like rowing machine and Airdyne sprints instead of cycling.

11:18 Two hard sets yield results with one-third the volume of conventional training
His strength structure is fixed: one light warm-up set, one medium set, then only two sets pushed to the edge of form breakdown, resting three to four minutes between. Per bodypart, just two or three movements. A multi-year soccer athlete testing his method reported it was one-third her previous volume but yielded results she found almost unbelievable.

21:35 Blue light sensitivity varies enormously; your skepticism might actually be justified
On pre-sleep blue light, Huberman notes enormous individual variation: some people spike cortisol and lose sleep from barely-visible light even through closed eyelids; others are completely insensitive, for reasons still unclear and independent of eye color. He mentions Marc Andreessen publicly saying he quit alcohol but dismisses blue-light protection entirely—Huberman acknowledges individual variation is real.

26:43 One supplement cuts infection risk by more than half in flu exposure studies
He cites a study exposing people to flu virus: those taking placebo infected at over 70%, while those taking N-acetylcysteine (NAC, a glutathione precursor) infected at just over 20%. He takes one dose daily himself, escalating to three when he feels illness coming or sees others sick.

30:55 Your social media phone needs to be locked away, not just silenced
Huberman admits social media is his weakest point: he keeps X and Instagram on a separate phone locked in a ‘super-prison-grade’ safe, accessible only at set times. He says this embarrasses him—ideally humans should self-regulate. He cites research: even with phone in a backpack, powered off, or under a chair, the brain burns extra cognitive resources to maintain equivalent focus. Phone completely absent, those resources release.

37:18 Peak cognitive windows contain exponentially more value than makeup work done later
For him, the two best cognitive windows are roughly 9:30 am to 12:30 pm and 4:35 pm to 7 pm—but the window varies per person, and he advises everyone to find theirs. The core warning: if work during that peak window is diverted to company-unrelated matters, the loss isn't just those three or four hours. Output during that window is exponentially higher than output from makeup work done later, and it also compresses personal time.

46:30 Startups are endurance races that demand weekly reset to avoid burnout
Huberman relays neuroscientist Bob Knight's early advice: first determine your daily maximum sustainable work output, then find a restorative method to reset once a week—Knight fishes, Huberman hikes and socializes. He notes that people who run on high stimulation continuously tend to be the ones who disappear last; sustaining intensity matters as much as the intensity itself.

item.title: The government tried to break up his family business with estate tax, so he moved to Bermuda to keep control
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-03-knowledge-政府想用遗产税拆散家族企业-他干脆移居百慕大保住控制权/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-03-knowledge-政府想用遗产税拆散家族企业-他干脆移居百慕大保住控制权/
item.description: K.C. Irving lived by one rule for sixty years: everything that matters must stay under your control. When new tax laws first threatened that 100% ownership, he chose to leave New Brunswick with his entire fortune.
item.content:encoded:
K.C. Irving lived by one rule for sixty years: everything that matters must stay under your control. When new tax laws first threatened that 100% ownership, he chose to leave New Brunswick with his entire fortune.

For anyone trying to understand how family businesses use vertical integration and refuse to dilute ownership to build a moat—especially the Senate hearing and the Bermuda move, which show how concentrated control ultimately traps you at the scale you've built.

12:30 He buried a gas tank without his father's permission
At nineteen, Irving saw automobiles appearing on country roads where Eaton mail-order catalogs could deliver clothing and tools but not gasoline. He registered his family's general store as an Imperial Oil agent without asking his father. At dawn one summer morning in 1920, before the village woke, he dug a hole and buried a 250-gallon tank. When his father demanded to know what he was doing, Irving answered shovel in hand: "We will absolutely not simply shut our doors." This was his first display of a lifetime pattern: finding positions no one else occupied and claiming them.

16:40 When his supplier cut him off, he found new oil and blended his own
As business boomed, Imperial Oil cut off Irving's supply to force him to sell only cars. He didn't negotiate—he found a new supplier in Tulsa, Oklahoma, had gasoline shipped by rail in tank cars, and ordered a storage tank 40 times the size of his original 250-gallon one. By coincidence, Imperial also ordered the same model tank for its own station, and both arrived in the same small town on the same day. He branded his antifreeze blend Primrose, splicing together the names Premier and White Rose to declare war, and soon captured 95% of the town's gasoline business.

32:29 The railroad choked him off, so he bought a ship
In 1932, a government-owned railroad imposed higher freight rates, arguing that "Imperial Oil has its own refinery and you don't." After two years of negotiation and a final ultimatum that was refused, the railroad counted on him to accept—or at most to buy an oil tanker, which no one would do in the Great Depression. Irving bought the tanker anyway and built his own dock a mile from the railroad's headquarters, then invited the entire town to watch it dock. It ran aground in mud. Irving grabbed a shovel and worked alongside the crew until 2:30 a.m., when they finally freed it.

48:07 Before buying forest land, he put on snowshoes and counted trees himself
Irving's office desk connected to a private radio network that reached his factories, ships, and gas stations directly. Before buying 700,000 acres of forest, he didn't simply sign after hearing the expert report. He put on snowshoes and walked into the woods with a forestry expert to count trees by hand. Back at camp each night, they compared tallies. If the numbers didn't match, they counted again the next day until both sides aligned. Only then did he write the check. He also made a habit of appearing unannounced at his plants in the middle of the night—the best way to understand a business, he said, was to know its beginning and end and every link in between, so you could make sound decisions.

59:34 He took 96% of the deal, then asked about the 4% left behind
Harrison McCain spent eighteen months landing a major client and called Irving in excitement with the news, expecting praise. Irving asked only: "Did you get the lubricant business?" McCain hadn't—it accounted for just 4% of the total deal. Irving cared not about the 96% they'd won, but the 4% they'd lost. McCain later distilled what he'd learned from Irving into a single sentence: Never be satisfied. McCain also said that Irving's name alone was enough to make counterparts concede before negotiations even began.

1:08:58 His refusal of BP's control clause was vindicated by the Suez Crisis
British Petroleum agreed to build a refinery with Irving in Saint John, and after settling the terms, added a condition: BP would have the right to buy out Irving Oil after Irving retired or died. Irving had three sons to pass the business to—he refused. Months later, Standard Oil got blocked by the Suez Crisis; Arab oil couldn't flow, so tankers had to sail around Africa, requiring deep-water ports. Saint John never froze and had the depth needed. This geopolitical event, seemingly unrelated, finally closed the refinery deal Irving had been waiting twenty-three years to make. He called it the best deal he'd ever negotiated.

1:41:52 A Senate question revealed his power exceeded the province itself
A federal senator accused the Irving family of monopolizing all English-language newspapers in New Brunswick and summoned Irving to testify in Ottawa. The senator asked: "If something harms New Brunswick, does it harm your business?" Irving answered: "Yes." The senator pressed: "Then if something harms your business, does it harm New Brunswick?" Irving again: "Yes." Those two affirmations trapped him in the very trap he'd spent forty years building. He'd spent a lifetime freeing himself from dependence on anyone, yet now the entire province had become dependent on him.

1:46:04 When the new inheritance tax was announced, he moved to Bermuda
Starting in 1972, Canada would tax capital gains; New Brunswick wanted to add an estate tax on top. Nearly all of Irving's wealth was locked in private company shares—refineries, paper mills, ships—with no public market where his sons could sell shares to pay a bill at that scale. To spare his sons from having to dismantle everything he'd built, on December 23, 1971, he and his wife quietly flew to Bermuda and thereafter strictly limited the days they spent in Canada. His only public statement: "I am no longer a resident of New Brunswick. My sons are managing the operations."

item.title: War museums display heroes' photographs, but not a single victim's face
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-03-throughline-战争博物馆里挂满英雄照-却没有一张受害者/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-03-throughline-战争博物馆里挂满英雄照-却没有一张受害者/
item.description: Noah Adams observed in Belgrade's military museum: two hours of exhibits from ninth-century bows to World War II tanks, all heroic images, not one photograph of victims—making war itself seem like the normal state of affairs.
item.content:encoded:
Noah Adams observed in Belgrade's military museum: two hours of exhibits from ninth-century bows to World War II tanks, all heroic images, not one photograph of victims—making war itself seem like the normal state of affairs.

This is a tribute to NPR veteran broadcaster Noah Adams, reprising three of his pieces from 1993, 1998, and 2001. The density is light but the observation is sharp—a perfect listen for careful readers who appreciate close, writerly attention to detail.

1:04 War museums display heroes' photographs but never display victims' faces
When Noah Adams visited Yugoslavia's military museum at Karamagdan Park in Belgrade, fresh from a two-week reporting trip to Serbia, he found himself looking at two hours of exhibits spanning from ninth-century bows to World War II artillery and tanks. What struck him was the absence: only heroic images hung in the gallery; not a single photograph of a victim appeared. Combined with the daily news from the Bosnian War—young people dying, politicians speaking, relief organizations intervening, the cycle repeating—the museum seemed to suggest that war itself was simply the normal state of things.

4:13 Old men playing chess in the park harbor decades of unspeakable silence
In that same park, Adams watched elderly men playing chess with each other, neat in appearance and gentle with one another. He guessed that among them were men who, fifty years ago, had fought in what was called the ‘人民解放战争’ during World War II. But he acknowledged his own limitation: two weeks in Serbia was not enough to truly understand the Bosnian War. Instead, he turned to an American parallel. If a Serbian came to America, how would you explain that Gettysburg saw 40,000 deaths and Antietam 24,000? And he noticed something else: Serbs who publicly opposed the Bosnian War would, the moment Kosovo's Albanians came up in conversation, show a different look in their eyes altogether.

10:30 At age ten, a frightened horse dragged his father to his death
In 1998, during Nebraska's severe drought, Adams interviewed Glenn Osborn, a farmer born in 1919. Osborn recalled the dust storms of the Depression era: chickens would return to their coops in mid-afternoon because the air was full of ash; the sky turned dark as night. But there was heavier loss in his past. His mother died when he was five. At ten, he went with his father to a neighbor's to husk corn. A truck fitted with a canvas cover passed by, and the wind caught the canvas, startling the horses pulling it. His father ran after the horses, while young Glenn ran behind a box. The horses dragged his father to death. Sixty years later, when Osborn recounted this, he said it felt ‘就像昨天早上才发生的’as though it had happened only yesterday morning.

14:34 Farm crisis hotlines reopen when drought threatens farmers' mental survival
Drought destroys more than crops. It tears at farmers' mental states. Jim Osborn and his wife Lynn recalled that the farm crisis hotline—set up during the bank failures of the 1980s—was running again. Because many farmers were experiencing acute stress and crisis. Adams pressed: did the USDA really operate a phone crisis line because farmers were considering suicide? The answer was yes. Lynn added that when such moments came, it was usually the farmer's wife who made the call; the farmers themselves preferred not to talk face-to-face with anyone. They would rather go home and sit alone facing a wall in silent anguish.

17:40 No customers at the hardware store means the drought is here
Benkelman, population 1,193, depends entirely on the agriculture surrounding it. Erma Johnson, who runs the hardware store, explained that she carries roughly one hundred accounts on credit, and nearly all of them are farmers. You don't need to check the weather forecast; just see if customers walk in the door. If they don't, there's a drought. Pat Rotherman, the town bank's president, gave harder numbers: this year, he estimated that ten to fifteen percent of small farmers wouldn't make it—they would have to sell their land and exit farming. In normal years, that figure should be zero. The bank's approach was to try to keep them, not push them into bankruptcy.

19:44 Free barbecue night, and then the rain came that changed everything
On the third night of the county fair, the wind picked up. The American Legion flag they'd just bought whipped tight. Clouds piled high to the north, west, and south. It was Free Barbecue Night: a thousand people stood in line for grilled beef, onions, and potatoes. When thunder rolled, nobody left early—nobody wanted to go, even as the fair had to close ahead of schedule and the concert moved into the high school auditorium. The next morning at breakfast, farmers swapped rain stories. One household had measured one-quarter inch; another two inches. Almost every farm had two rain gauges to cross-check. This single rainfall became the week's only big news in Benkelman—not fit to print in the Denver Post, but the only story that truly mattered to the town.

22:50 The researchers themselves won't say their gene edits are safe for cats
In 2001, Adams interviewed David Avner, president of Transgenic Pets, a company developing cats through genetic engineering that wouldn't trigger human allergies. The plan was to disable the gene that makes the protein in cats' sebaceous glands that causes the allergy. Adams asked the obvious question: over the course of evolution, might cats actually need this gene? Avner called it redundant protein, said they'd researched it for ten to fifteen years, and believed it should be fine. But Adams caught a crucial detail: when the same question was put to Jerry Yang, a genetics professor at the University of Connecticut who'd worked on the project, Yang's answer was: ‘我们希望不会’We hope it won't. Adams noted directly that this sounded nothing like confidence.

23:50 Hypoallergenic cats would be priced from $750 to $1,000 each
For this technology still in development, Avner provided specific commercial projections and pricing: the company hoped to breed the first hypoallergenic cats by 2003 and, in the early years of mass production, bring the price down to $750 to $1,000 per cat—affordable for ordinary households. He positioned the technology as a paradigm shift in allergy treatment: instead of managing immune responses with antihistamines and weekly desensitization shots, you could simply remove the allergen source itself.

item.title: Regulated verse meter was how aristocratic hierarchy got formalized into poetry
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-03-cn2aa250-近体诗平仄格律-本质是贵族社会的等级礼仪搬进了诗歌/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-03-cn2aa250-近体诗平仄格律-本质是贵族社会的等级礼仪搬进了诗歌/
item.description: Discovering Chinese's four tones in the Yongming era launched regulated verse, but what truly crystallized it was aristocratic logic: everyone must fit precisely into rank. Bland content counted as poetry if meter was correct; brilliance meant nothing if tones misaligned.
item.content:encoded:
Discovering Chinese's four tones in the Yongming era launched regulated verse, but what truly crystallized it was aristocratic logic: everyone must fit precisely into rank. Bland content counted as poetry if meter was correct; brilliance meant nothing if tones misaligned.

Threads Southern Qi's military origins, fiscal transformation, and the birth of regulated verse meter into one narrative—high density for readers trying to understand how aristocratic hierarchy structured itself through every institution.

8:10 The poet who invented regulated verse rules was simultaneously trying to overthrow the heir
Wang Rong descended from the greatest aristocratic family of the south—sixth-generation heir of Wang Dao—and co-led the Yongming tonal movement alongside Shen Yue and Xie Zhuang. Yet he also plotted to install Crown Prince Xiao Ziliang as emperor when Xiao Ze lay dying. Dressed in armor with sword drawn, he positioned himself at the palace gates to execute the coup. He failed, and was executed. It was this contradiction that drew scholar Lin Xiaoguang to make Wang Rong, rather than Shen Yue, the subject of his doctoral research: the aristocratic poet who was also the regime's most dangerous conspirator.

13:54 Poverty and military lineage gave the Xiao family both obsessive hunger and battlefield hardness
Before the Xiao family rose to power, they carried four compounded disadvantages in Southern Dynasty society. They were 寒門—the lowest tier within the gentry, but gentry nonetheless. They were a military lineage, useful for conquest but suppressed in peacetime. They were economically destitute despite aristocratic rank, since wealth and status were independent hierarchies. They gained initial favor only through affinal connection when one branch became empress dowager. Poverty scarred them. Once poverty-scarred, they became obsessed with money and desperate to get rich. But poverty also taught them something: the hard capability that comes from fighting at the bottom. This combination made them formidable.

27:23 Xiao Ze's first brilliant military move was abandoning the city to hold the region
Early in his career, Xiao Ze served as magistrate in Nankang, Jiangxi, when the Liu Zixun rebellion erupted. His father Xiao Daocheng was already commanding forces near the capital. Xiao Ze refused to surrender and was imprisoned by the regional inspector. His family's household retainers—forty-some people, some accounts say over a hundred—broke through the jail and freed him, including Huankang, who later became a general so fearsome that people said his portrait could cure malaria: anyone with fever who saw it would be so startled they'd recover. Recognizing that enemy reinforcements were approaching, Xiao Ze made a counterintuitive choice: abandon the city he'd just seized and withdraw into the mountains of northern Guangdong, where he conducted guerrilla operations. When enemy forces retreated, he returned to take the city again, having used his retreat to tie down enemy reserves.

40:34 A servant wearing the crown prince's robes nearly toppled the heir to power
As heir, Xiao Ze lived with ostentatious excess and gifted the robes designated for the crown prince to his favored attendant Zhang Jingzhen. When Zhang Jingzhen sailed past on a boat, people on shore mistook him for the heir himself. Word reached Xiao Daocheng, who exploded with rage. In ancient society, hierarchy was visually reinforced—you could tell someone's rank at a glance. Everything was calibrated by status, everything divided by rank. Zhang Jingzhen's act suggested the heir was preparing to usurp power. Xiao Daocheng considered removing him as heir. Zhang Jingzhen was executed to contain the crisis. But Xiao Daocheng hesitated before making the break final. General Wang Jingze forcibly pulled him from his bed and dragged him to the heir's lodge for leisurely conversation and games. The crisis passed.

56:46 Centralizing the state treasury impoverished common people even as the state grew wealthy
Under Late Song, military costs had emptied the central treasury while regional strongmen accumulated wealth—a pattern called ‘国贫民负’: the state was poor, powerful families rich. By the Yongming era, Xiao Ze reversed this through audits and other measures. Central reserves in copper coin accumulated to 500,000,000 by the end of Yongming. Xiao Ze's personal treasury held over 300,000,000—nearly equal to the state treasury itself. But this reversal came at a cost: common people saw no benefit, and as the state increased extraction to fuel its wealth accumulation, they grew poorer than before.

1:01:10 Tax audits hunted the wrong target and sparked the dynasty's only major rebellion
Southern Dynasty household registration faced two problems. One was inherited from the Eastern Jin and earlier: yellow and white registers separating locals from northern refugees, both groups having drifted outside formal taxation nearly 180 years before Yongming. By Yongming, this was stale. The real problem originated in the Yuan Jia era, when looser laws let gentry privileges be secretly expanded, and commoners bribed officials to claim gentry status and escape taxes. Xiao Ze's audits primarily targeted the second group. But officials at each level found ways to extract bribes, gutting the policy's effect. The audits ultimately provoked Tang Yu's rebellion—the only significant uprising during the Yongming era.

1:13:57 Regulated verse meter was not a musical discovery—it was etiquette codified as grammar
Scholars typically trace regulated verse to phonological discovery: the four tones of Chinese. Lin Xiaoguang argues differently. The Yongming tonal movement was not fundamentally about sound. It was about transplanting aristocratic logic into poetry—the obsession with hierarchy, propriety, and precise formal positioning. Just as courtiers debated what rank of mourning robes a prince with low-status birth should wear, poets now had to fit into strict tonal and parallelism rules. Bland content passed if it followed the meter; brilliant insight failed if tones didn't align or couplets weren't parallel. This was not technical progress in acoustics. This was aristocratic society writing its hierarchy into the grammar of verse.

1:21:04 Tang publicly destroyed the South's legacy while secretly copying its entire technique
Du Fu wrote ‘竊攀屈宋宜方駕, 恐與齊梁作後塵’—fearing the fate of Qi and Liang, the fallen Southern dynasties. This represented official Tang narrative: the South was a small defeated polity that had to be condemned. But when Tang editors compiled the Literary Anthology, they included thousands of passages from Southern literature, while Northern literature received only handfuls of entries. Tang's public judgment was political; its practice was apprenticeship. Lin Xiaoguang concludes that Southern poetry ‘上承騷賦, 下啟隋唐’—it inherited classical tradition and founded everything Tang poetry would become. The standard dismissal obscures the real story: the South was indispensable.

item.title: Polls aren't undercounting Republicans—they're overcorrecting from past misses
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-03-oddlots-民调不是在低估共和党-而是在怕错而过度修正/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-03-oddlots-民调不是在低估共和党-而是在怕错而过度修正/
item.description: A Maine poll used a ‘likely voter model’ to compress Democrats' raw 9-point lead to 2; Nate Silver says it's self-protection after 2016, not math.
item.content:encoded:
A Maine poll used a ‘likely voter model’ to compress Democrats' raw 9-point lead to 2; Nate Silver says it's self-protection after 2016, not math.

To understand how weak Trump's support truly is, whether polls deserve trust, and if AI can replace real-world polling, this episode packs information throughout.

2:04 Trump's approval hits lows unseen since Truman's era
Trump's approval sits around 37%—Nate Silver notes this is the worst approval rating for a sitting president at a midterm since Truman in 1946. Compare 2018: Trump's approval was higher then and gas was cheaper, yet Republicans still lost 41 House seats. He describes this election as ‘caught between a rock and a hard place’—the environment strongly favors Democrats, but to win the Senate, Democrats must flip Texas, Kansas, Alaska, and South Carolina: deep-red states where victory is mathematically necessary but a long shot.

4:09 Trump has exited campaign ads but seized the spotlight anyway
The clearest sign this is a referendum on Trump: Republican campaign ads have stopped mentioning him, Republican podcasts no longer discuss him. Yet Trump himself wants to grab center stage—he endorsed Texas's Ken Paxton and insisted on escalating toward conflict with Iran, moves that flipped a Senate map that could have been close into Democratic territory.

6:10 Polls underestimated Democrats when Trump wasn't on the ballot
Polls have systematically underestimated Trump himself in recent elections (2016, 2020, 2024), but in races where Trump isn't on the ballot—like last year's New Jersey and Virginia gubernatorial races—polls badly underestimated Democrats. One explanation: Trump mobilizes hard-to-reach, infrequent voters who won't turn out for downstream candidates like Kansas's Roger Marshall or Texas's Ken Paxton.

15:19 A Maine poll artificially compressed a 9-point lead into 2
Maine's Marist poll showed Democrat Troy Jackson ahead by 9 points in raw results, then dropped to just 2 points after applying the ‘likely voter model’; the gubernatorial lead fell from 11 points to zero. Nate Silver: the math doesn't add up—it's not that the model computed this result, but that pollsters chose a palatable number and reverse-engineered the parameters to reach it.

18:22 AI cannot serve as a real-world polling substitute through synthetic respondents
On the idea of using AI to generate synthetic respondents for polls, Nate Silver is blunt: polling is one of the few remaining sources of real-world data, and can't be outsourced to AI. He gives an example—ask a model to generate a ‘synthetic Latino respondent’ and 99% of synthetic answers will say they love soccer. It's like asking Claude to pick a number from 0 to 10 and it always picks 7: models output stereotype averages, not the messy reality where voters disagree even with themselves.

21:24 Gerrymandering to win more seats can backfire and cost seats
Nate Silver introduces the political term ‘dummymander’—a gerrymander designed to flip more seats that winds up costing your party seats instead. Florida's DeSantis drew maps based on presidential-year benchmarks and didn't account for this cycle's D+9 national environment; Texas Republicans bet Latino voters in South Texas had shifted red—if that gamble fails, the maps could backfire.

27:31 Campaign spending on ads faces steeply diminishing returns
On whether campaigns should spend money on ads or ground game, Nate Silver says ad returns diminish sharply. He cites Sam Bankman-Fried, who poured $10 million into an Oregon House primary without the candidate's consent, only to have voters bombarded with mail and spooked by backing from an ‘eccentric crypto billionaire’—the candidate lost badly.

37:46 AI compressed two and a half days of work into fifteen minutes
Last year, coding the complex NFL playoff tiebreaker rules by hand took Nate Silver two and a half days and still had bugs and missing rules. Now GPT or Claude handles it in fifteen minutes with code ten times faster. But he warns AI introduces subtle bugs—their football model once had a scoring loop that pointed backward in time, so 2026 ratings affected 1900 ratings, bizarre.

item.title: A four-year-old's months-long repeated expressions of sadness merit serious attention
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-03-secureattach-四岁孩子反复说自己难过长达数月-值得认真对待/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-03-secureattach-四岁孩子反复说自己难过长达数月-值得认真对待/
item.description: A four-year-old boy has spent months repeatedly saying he is sad without being able to explain why; a psychologist says this warrants professional evaluation—depression in young children is rare but real, and treatable.
item.content:encoded:
A four-year-old boy has spent months repeatedly saying he is sad without being able to explain why; a psychologist says this warrants professional evaluation—depression in young children is rare but real, and treatable.

For parents uncertain whether their child's emotional expression is normal, it offers concrete criteria for deciding whether to seek professional help—not generic reassurance.

4:06 Months of sadness is the key signal
This mother's four-year-old son has spent months repeatedly saying he is sad, sometimes the moment he wakes up. Rebecca Hershberg notes that even four-year-olds—and younger children—can experience depression. While young children rarely meet the formal diagnostic criteria for depression, a duration of ‘months’ is already a long span for a four-year-old. Add the mother's own long struggle with anxiety and depression: that family-level genetic loading is a variable beyond parenting style's control. With both factors present, Hershberg recommends direct professional evaluation rather than waiting for the podcast to air before offering guidance.

7:15 Depression in young children is rare but treatable
Host Sarah Bren cautions against panic at the word ‘depression’—it is genuinely rare in young children, and even if evaluation confirms it, it is entirely treatable. She frames the process as elimination, not crisis, aiming for parents to neither dismiss the signal nor fear seeking help. Her view: failing to screen is the riskier choice.

8:18 Appetite, sleep, and peer relationships tell the story
There is no single formula for whether to intervene, but Rebecca gives concrete dimensions to observe: the child's appetite, sleep, and how they interact with peers. She even recommends ruling out seemingly unrelated physical factors—children with prolonged low mood sometimes need thyroid screening. The pediatrician is the easiest first stop, though most are not mental-health experts and can only make preliminary judgments before deciding on referral.

9:20 The change from baseline matters more than the emotion itself
Sarah adds that what matters is not whether a child says ‘sad’ but whether this represents a departure from their baseline—a shift in how they engage with the world, versus a temperamental constant. Typical departure signals are changes in relationships, loss of interest, and giving up things they once loved. The mother's description partly fits this pattern.

11:28 Age thresholds matter when finding a child therapist
Rebecca cautions that many who claim to do child therapy only accept ages six and up. Therapists who actually treat preschoolers should explicitly state expertise with young and toddler-age children. For this age group, therapy is nearly always play-based—stories, stuffed animals, puppets, not sitting down to talk. Parents must actively confirm the therapist's experience covers this age.

16:42 Play therapy works for internalizing problems, not externalizing ones
Rebecca distinguishes two types: children who internalize emotions—sadness, anxiety, trauma—the ‘internalizing’ problems play therapy excels at; and those with ‘externalizing’ behavior problems like aggression or impulsivity, where play therapy struggles to transfer learning from the room to the world, often requiring family-system intervention. She urges parents to be ‘informed consumers’ because some therapists claim to handle all types.

19:50 Parental presence is the safety net that makes therapy work
For children this young, Rebecca more often uses joint parent-child play therapy rather than having the child meet alone. She calls parental presence a ‘warm handoff’: the child experiences the therapist as safe, with the parent as a reference point. When discussing painful material, knowing both mother and therapist are ‘there’ lets the young child enter genuine emotional work with a stranger.

item.title: Glanders still has no vaccine; culling all infected animals remains the only control method
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-03-tpwky-鼻疽至今没有疫苗-防控唯一办法就是扑杀所有感染动物/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-03-tpwky-鼻疽至今没有疫苗-防控唯一办法就是扑杀所有感染动物/
item.description: This bacterium, which obligately parasitizes equines, kills over 90% of those infected, is inherently antibiotic-resistant, and after more than a century of human research, the only effective approach remains: discover and cull.
item.content:encoded:
This bacterium, which obligately parasitizes equines, kills over 90% of those infected, is inherently antibiotic-resistant, and after more than a century of human research, the only effective approach remains: discover and cull.

Obscure pathogen education with high information density but inclined toward curiosity value; well-researched historical detail on Civil War cavalry plague; better suited for curiosity-driven listening than policy reference.

3:05 A doctor took three weeks to admit he had contracted glanders
In 1911, a Punjab Veterinary College researcher was already familiar with the appearance of typical glanders cultures—he used this evidence every year to order the culling of infected horses. But when the same bacterial colony appeared in a culture from his own wound, he convinced himself ‘it must be a mistake,’ and even destroyed the already-prepared sample, until the disease progressed to undeniable severity. He subsequently underwent 45 operations (27 under general anesthesia), with illness lasting from March 1911 until June 1913 before recovery—and he relapsed once after that.

9:40 The lethal glanders bacterium carries roughly 1200 fewer genes than its relative
Burkholderia mallei, the pathogen of glanders, is an obligate parasite that can barely survive independently outside its host—a stark contrast to the related Burkholderia pseudomallei (which causes melioidosis and freely survives and reproduces in soil), whose genome is roughly 1200 genes larger than mallei. Though mallei has ‘degenerated’ into an obligate parasite, that same adaptation makes it vulnerable to deliberate eradication across entire regions, as happened in the twentieth century.

20:57 Glanders is never treated; infected animals are only culled
When animals contract glanders, the World Organisation for Animal Health recommends direct culling rather than antibiotic treatment—the bacterium is inherently resistant to most antibiotics. More extreme: any individual exposed to an infected animal faces continuous monitoring, and at the first symptom has the same fate as the animal. The approach is crude, but it is the only method that actually works; the cost is that no one can now say what the true natural mortality rate is in infected animals, because almost every case ends by human termination before it could run its natural course.

24:00 Treated humans still die in forty percent to fifty percent of cases
After human infection with glanders, the untreated mortality rate exceeds 90%; the pneumonic form typically proves fatal within 10 to 30 days. Even with treatment, mortality remains as high as 40%-50%. Because the disease is so rare, the Infectious Diseases Society of America has no official treatment guideline; existing protocols amount to expert consensus only: at least 10 to 14 days of intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics, followed by six months to a year of oral antibiotics, without necessarily requiring drainage of internal abscesses—entirely unlike standard care for most bacterial infections.

34:21 A student died dissecting a glanders-infected horse, yet the professor blamed cadaverous poison
Into the nineteenth century, whether glanders was contagious remained a centuries-old dispute in veterinary medicine. In 1817, a veterinary student accidentally cut his hand while dissecting a glanders-infected horse and died shortly after. The professor investigating took samples from the student's body and inoculated them into two donkeys, both of which became infected with glanders—yet he concluded that glanders was not contagious and the student had died of ‘cadaverous poisoning’ (which was actually glanders itself). This dispute only ended in the mid-nineteenth century through a series of experimental infections.

41:35 A single Union cavalry depot lost seventeen thousand horses to glanders in one year
During the Civil War, the Union lost over 284,000 horses and mules in just the first two years. To centralize supply, both sides built massive depots holding tens of thousands of horses—the Giesboro depot in Washington, D.C. could hold 30,000 horses at peak capacity. Horses greet each other nose-to-nose and share feeding troughs, providing ideal conditions for glanders transmission. From January 1864 to April 1865, that single depot lost 17,000 horses to disease alone—on one day, over 180 died. The Confederacy fared worse: one depot received 7,000 horses and sent only 1,000 to the battlefield.

48:43 A Tier 1 bioterror agent, glanders infected a microbiologist in a lab this century
During World War II, Japanese forces deployed glanders in biological attacks against horses, civilians, and prisoners of war; there are also reports that the Soviet Union deliberately infected mujahideen horses during the Afghan War in the early 1980s. In 2000, the United States formally classified glanders as a Tier 1 select agent, placing it alongside smallpox, plague, anthrax, and Ebola. Ironically, that same year, a 33-year-old microbiologist at the U.S. Army Medical Research Institute of Infectious Diseases accidentally contracted glanders while researching it—he frequently worked without gloves, marking the first recorded human case in English medical literature since 1949; he survived after six months of treatment.

51:51 Vaccine research remains at animal testing; glanders persists in multiple regions
Glanders has been eradicated from vast regions including the EU, Australia, and the United States, but through culling and isolation alone, not vaccination—animal vaccine research remains at early experimental stages, without even Phase 1 human trials. Meanwhile, glanders continues to cause sporadic cases and outbreaks in South Asia, Southwest Asia, and North Africa: a 2010 Tehran Zoo outbreak killed 4 lions and 1 tiger; Nepal's first confirmed case came in 2022; Brazil reported 120 cases across 43 municipalities between 2020 and 2024.

item.title: Parents' accommodation of avoidance makes anxiety harder to treat
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-03-asklisa-父母越是心疼着接送孩子逃避-焦虑就越难治好/

item.category: Ask Lisa: The Psychology of Raising Tweens & Teens
item.description: The relief from avoidance teaches the brain ‘I can't handle this,’ making escape likelier next time. The evidence-based approach is gradual exposure to discomfort—a framework that works equally for everyday nervousness and clinical anxiety disorder.
item.content:encoded:
The relief from avoidance teaches the brain ‘I can't handle this,’ making escape likelier next time. The evidence-based approach is gradual exposure to discomfort—a framework that works equally for everyday nervousness and clinical anxiety disorder.

Through a real letter, it distinguishes three diagnostic markers of clinical anxiety from everyday nervousness, and reveals well-intentioned parental responses that inadvertently perpetuate the anxiety cycle.

3:08 Three markers distinguish everyday nervousness from diagnosable anxiety
Clinicians apply three hard metrics: functional impairment (whether anxiety disrupts daily life, like the letter-writer's daughter being picked up from school repeatedly mid-day), degree of suffering (crying, anguish), and duration (persisting weeks rather than resolving in days). All three together signal need for professional intervention—not mere introversion or temporary setback.

5:08 We use one word for two separate psychological conditions
Psychology should have distinct vocabularies for everyday nervousness and clinical anxiety disorder, but it doesn't. The word ‘anxiety’ both flattens everything and pathologizes it all. Elkins uses a water-glass metaphor: everyone is born with some baseline anxiety water; it serves a function, keeping you safe (look both ways before crossing, brush teeth before a date). Only when the glass overflows—due to genetics and other factors—does clinical anxiety disorder emerge.

13:23 The temporary relief of avoidance teaches permanent anxiety
Each time discomfort is escaped rather than faced, the brain learns: feeling better came from running away, therefore ‘I cannot handle this.’ Next time something similar arises, anxiety intensifies and avoidance becomes likelier. In the letter, the girl ducking into the bathroom and being picked up looks like relief to parents—but it reinforces ‘I'm alone, unloved, friendless.’

14:23 Exposure therapy starts with the smallest manageable discomfort
