The gold-standard psychological treatment for anxiety is exposure therapy—ranking situations by distress level from least to most, starting with the easiest (greeting one classmate in the classroom), then gradually climbing, not throwing the child into full-day school as the first step. Elkins jokes her program ‘isn't a spa’—kids typically feel worse at first, which is precisely how you know the method is working.

22:45 Years of avoidance can transform ordinary anxiety into phobia
Elkins shared her own story: years in Boston and Manhattan meant she never needed to drive—not deliberate avoidance, but functionally she stopped. When she finally had to, while pregnant and terrified, it happened in Massachusetts, notorious for dangerous roads. Her solution: drive repeatedly until it felt boring—a finish line everyone can reach, but only after tolerating initial discomfort.

28:06 Parents are the real leverage point in treating child anxiety
Therapeutic rapport accounts for up to 50% of clinical outcomes, but even if a child refuses to see a therapist, parents aren't helpless. The most exciting progress of the past decade is ‘parent-directed’ treatment like Yale's SPACE program: the patient is the child, but the therapist primarily coaches parents, helping them spot well-meaning responses that accidentally reinforce the child's anxiety cycle.

32:21 Accommodation motivated by kindness perpetuates the anxiety cycle
Accommodation means parents adjusting their own behavior to reduce the child's distress—no parent sets out to fan the flames, but anxiety hijacks parents' deepest instinct to ease pain, making accommodation invisible and continuous. Research shows the more parents accommodate, the worse children's anxiety disorder tends to become; and those same parents suffer more depression, anxiety, and stress themselves—bad news for everyone.

38:35 Switching schools won't help without addressing the avoidance pattern
When parents wrestle with whether to transfer their child, Elkins is cautious, because anxiety is an ‘opportunist’—it will seize any chance to destroy one lifestyle and escape to the next. Without first addressing the underlying anxiety cycle and family accommodation patterns, a new school just teaches avoidance as the go-to coping strategy. Transfer should only come first if there's genuine, ongoing bullying, harassment, discrimination, or safety threats.

item.title: Two-year-old defiance isn't a broken bond—it's emotion doing repair work
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-03-unruffled-两岁娃的疯狂抵抗不是亲子关系出问题-而是情绪在自愈/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-03-unruffled-两岁娃的疯狂抵抗不是亲子关系出问题-而是情绪在自愈/
item.description: When toddlers say no to everything—getting in the car, bathing, holding hands at crossings—it's because they've weathered massive changes with no sense of control; the answer isn't more choices but tighter, earlier boundaries.
item.content:encoded:
When toddlers say no to everything—getting in the car, bathing, holding hands at crossings—it's because they've weathered massive changes with no sense of control; the answer isn't more choices but tighter, earlier boundaries.

Two real letters show end-to-end resistance at boarding the car, bathing, holding hands, and bedtime, with ready-to-use response tactics.

5:10 Emotional storms are not signals of relationship breakdown
Her daughter experienced housing moves, then a new daycare within three weeks. Janet notes that same-aged and older children create more uncertainty than adults do—adding another source of stress. This is a ‘transition crisis,’ not a relationship problem. Better housing or warmer caregiving wouldn't prevent it. The trigger is loss of familiarity, regardless of circumstances.

6:11 Children who hold it together most need permission to collapse
Janet distinguishes two response patterns: fragile children break down directly, while determined, sensitive children ‘hold, hold, hold’—using continuous resistance to fight the out-of-control feeling. When parents worry about resistance and treat it as a red flag, they undermine the firmness these children need to release fear and sadness. Firmness is the container that enables the release.

9:22 During transitions, tighten boundaries rather than expand choices
The parent has been minimizing restrictions and offering choices, but Janet names a counterintuitive rule: in high-stakes transitions—boarding the car, crossing streets—children actually need fewer choices and earlier, clearer boundaries, not more autonomy. Set boundaries earlier and the resistance drops, because she won't have to wrestle alone with that feeling of lost control.

11:25 Set a window, then step in directly; no open delays
Specific tactics: at boarding time, offer a few seconds to choose, then directly buckle her in without prolonging the request loop. If she stands in the stroller, lift her without repeated verbal requests. When she heads the wrong way or toward danger, hold her hand or pick her up. Early intervention, more protection. At this stage, it won't hurt her—it's exactly what she needs.

14:28 Let kids choose bathing, but allow bedtime meltdowns
Bathing is a voluntary activity. If she refuses, wiping off works fine—let her choose. But stop dangerous or excessive behavior immediately by lifting her out. Bedtime is different. Children often save a full day's accumulated frustrations for this moment. Parents shouldn't add more books or extend delays to soothe. Instead, clearly allow the breakdown—this is exactly when she most needs to release.

15:31 Managing conflict with firmness and empathy strengthens the bond
The parent worried ‘the relationship will revolve around these conflicts.’ Janet's answer: when you meet intense feeling with both firmness and empathy, conflict actually fortifies rather than erodes the bond. It's not a warm, close moment. It's something deeper: the child confirming ‘I can have a huge feeling, and you're still here keeping me safe.’ It's one of the most connective things that happens between you.

17:34 Dramatic tears at separation signal secure attachment, not anxiety
Mom started a new job; dad now does daycare drop-off. Her goodbye to mom is intensely theatrical. Janet reframes this: when a child releases strong emotion at parting, it means there's enough safety with that parent to express pain. Dad may not see this intensity because the child experiences separations differently with him. This dramatic release is worth reading as a vote of confidence, not as evidence separation went wrong.

22:50 Asking for water and the bathroom is stalling the crash
The second letter: son goes from calm to suddenly ‘flipping a switch’ at bedtime, then repeatedly requesting water, the bathroom, finally collapsing in tears wanting to leave the room. Parent isn't sure whether reading more books soothes or teaches ‘emotions are scary; we can't handle them.’ Janet's suggestion: weave those routine requests into the presleep sequence, then you can confidently refuse extras. Then receive the tears as healthy release. The calmer parents are with this as normal, the faster it passes.

item.title: Fear of rejection is neurological: hyperactive amygdala, sluggish prefrontal cortex
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-03-goodinside-怕被拒绝不是矫情-杏仁核过度警觉-前额叶跟不上/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-03-goodinside-怕被拒绝不是矫情-杏仁核过度警觉-前额叶跟不上/
item.description: Psychologist Sasha Hamdani explains that fear of rejection is not a character flaw but a genuine neurological response—the result of an overactive amygdala and sluggish prefrontal cortex. Logic alone cannot override it.
item.content:encoded:
Psychologist Sasha Hamdani explains that fear of rejection is not a character flaw but a genuine neurological response—the result of an overactive amygdala and sluggish prefrontal cortex. Logic alone cannot override it.

For parents with sensitive children who spiral over read receipts—this episode offers concrete methods for identifying and responding, not just empty reassurance.

3:11 A concerned comment spiraled into a story of total ruin
During a TEDx talk, Sasha fell on stage. Her husband embraced her afterward, shirt soaked in sweat. When she asked why, he said, "I was so nervous for you." Within seconds, her brain had rewritten this: he thought her talk was terrible, the fall would destroy her career. She admits that in that moment, no words could have talked her out of it—her nervous system had already reacted before reason could intervene.

7:13 Rejection is chemical, not just a feeling or flaw
Rejection Sensitive Dysphoria (RSD) is not metaphorical but a neurological cascade triggered by real or perceived rejection and criticism. The key: even if the threat exists only in perception, not in reality, the body's physiological response is absolutely real. This is why "you're overreacting" fails completely—the person's amygdala actually is firing, their stress hormones actually are flooding their system, and the alarm is genuinely real to their nervous system.

9:19 The amygdala shouts while the prefrontal cortex lags behind
Neurologically, highly sensitive people show two brain abnormalities: an overactive amygdala (the threat detector) and an underresponsive prefrontal cortex (the reasoning center). The result is reactions that jump from zero to 60, wildly disproportionate to what triggered them. It's not a character flaw—it's that the emotional brain is at full volume while the thinking brain is too quiet to correct it.

16:46 Praise for another child becomes evidence she's less loved
When Sasha's daughter hears praise directed at her brother or another child, she instantly interprets it as "they'd rather have that child instead." She stops wanting to play basketball, walks away. Sasha doesn't force an explanation—she lets her daughter's amygdala cool down first. Then she offers unrelated praise: "You had a great idea moving the basketball hoop by the trash can." Only after reconnecting this way does she ask what her daughter actually fears: that her brother is better and there's no point in trying.

27:16 A period at the end of a text signals rejection
Sasha admits to extreme sensitivity to punctuation in messages. A period at the end? She reads it as "you hate me, we're done." Only exclamation points feel safe. She attributes this to how deeply feeling people assign meaning to ambiguity: reply speed, tone, punctuation all get converted into evidence of what the other person actually thinks of her. This interpretation system rarely matches reality, but it runs constantly.

28:21 Three words of agreement get rewritten as pure resentment
A mother texts another mom to ask about carpooling. The response: "that's fine." Instantly she spirals: "Does she not like my kid? Is she complaining about me to other moms?" Sasha's point: separate the signal from the story. "My body is reacting" and "what my body thinks that reaction means" are different things. The other mom was probably just busy—three words cannot carry an entire narrative of rejection. When they talked later, every assumption was wrong.

36:36 The thing that makes her suffer could be her gift
When her daughter worried about a smell in the garage, Sasha didn't say "there's no smell, stop being dramatic." Instead she said, "You're a super sensor. You notice things other people miss." She compares this to great comedians—they catch life's details because they're deeply feeling people. This doesn't deny that sensitivity causes pain. It acknowledges the pain is real, then connects that same wiring to a strength.

45:55 Rehearsing the worst words before they arrive softens the blow
After Dr. Becky returns from a book tour, her children are often distant or resentful. This hits her two deepest fears: that she's been replaced, and that they feel abandoned (a fear rooted in their father's 2024 death from lung cancer, when she was frequently away). They call this practice "emotional vaccination." Imagine the words you most dread hearing when you walk through the door. When those words actually come, the pain drops from a 10 to an 8—still real, but no longer devastating.

item.title: The biggest engineering challenge in legal AI is not models—it's data you can never see
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-02-latentspace-法律ai最大的工程难题不是模型-是永远看不到真实数据/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-02-latentspace-法律ai最大的工程难题不是模型-是永远看不到真实数据/
item.description: Most client data isn't even visible to the law firm itself. Legora's evals team has to guess what lawyers actually do, working only with classified and rewritten synthetic data.
item.content:encoded:
Most client data isn't even visible to the law firm itself. Legora's evals team has to guess what lawyers actually do, working only with classified and rewritten synthetic data.

High information density. Shows exactly how enterprise AI companies do evals, model selection, and frontline support in zero-visibility environments, with minimal filler.

10:43 The hardest hire: lawyers from top firms who can code
Legora's evals team blends engineers and lawyers, plus a distinct group of legal engineers—lawyers with CS backgrounds who spent three to four years at top firms. They're the hardest intersection to fill. Jacob calls them the company's hardest hire, but they're invaluable: they run evals and directly shape product design because they use the product every day and see clients every day. They become force multipliers who can summon a hundred-person expert pool to reshape the product.

14:30 AI may not be able to fix the law firm partnership model
Partnership exists because law firms' only capital is human capital—lose people, lose the firm, so just make people shareholders. Jacob argues AI should let firms codify experience and methods into reusable systems—say, a self-iterating knowledge graph—building firm-owned assets independent of any person. Instead, partners are paid by eating what they hunt, so encoding experience costs them clients. And those assets don't follow you when you leave partnership. The incentive misalignment has no answer yet.

16:45 Junior lawyers aren't disappearing—they're splitting into two tiers
The host suggests paralegals are obsolete, junior lawyers are obsolete. Jacob pushes back: that's not what they're seeing. He uses engineers as analogy: a great engineer is worth far more than two years ago because AI multiplies output; same for lawyers. Good junior lawyers become more valuable because AI lets them produce more, higher-quality work. This split always existed—now it's amplified, not the whole group gone.

26:40 Build evals when you cannot see a single user's real data
Legora's biggest engineering problem isn't model ability—it's that you can't see what customers do with the product. Data stays under lock. Often it doesn't even belong to the law firm; it belongs to their clients. Looking is forbidden. The company's only move is its evals team: guess, approximate real scenarios, build those guesses into test sets. Rewritten, anonymized synthetic traces are the only workaround. The stricter the anonymization, the weaker the signal. Jacob calls this the most maddening knot in the business.

28:50 Three years ago law firms wouldn't touch AWS
Legora runs entirely on Azure. Early in the company, law firm customers flatly didn't trust AWS or Google—no one had audited them. But Microsoft was already Office 365's vendor, so it had passed their audit test. Azure became the only option. In three years, that cloud skepticism nearly evaporated. Talk of private deployment vanished too. Legal's cloud migration was compressed into three years by AI pressure.

43:00 Legal engineers don't write code; frontline engineers do
Legora splits on-site support in two: legal engineers are big-firm alumni who know the product and customer workflows—they configure like power users, no code. Forward deployed engineers actually write code and hit customer APIs, usually serial entrepreneurs or large-company veterans. Big customers' custom needs go to legal engineers first; if they can't handle it and it needs product change or deep integration, escalate to forward engineers. This two-tier split lets the company staff big customers without assigning a full engineering team per customer.

50:00 Twenty engineers to beat everyone—he gave up that idea
Jacob once planned to keep the company to twenty engineers forever and beat much larger competitors. The team is now a hundred; he still thinks it's short. Hard competition and customer demand killed the minimalism. Now his thinking is different: collapse the product to a few core primitives—Lists, Projects, Agent. Customers think the company builds many things. Actually they're combinations of those three. He's even imagining a future where agents are themselves APIs, one agent call instead of a full interface to maintain.

1:03:50 Will large model companies squeeze out companies like Legora?
Anthropic and OpenAI have already squeezed out startups dependent on their models—once in code, once in search. Will legal be next? Jacob's read: no. Model companies must cover all enterprise knowledge work at once—law, data analysis, sales, finance. They can't go deep enough in one vertical. Small customers can use Claude for light legal work. But a $400 million acquisition? Enterprises pick the specialist.

item.title: Robot startups that won by selling hourly rates, not AI
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-02-a16z-机器人创业公司不卖ai-只卖-时薪16美元-这句话/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-02-a16z-机器人创业公司不卖ai-只卖-时薪16美元-这句话/
item.description: When Tutor pitches to first-time robot buyers, it never mentions models or AI—just one number: $16 an hour. The strategy reflects a vast market gap: America deploys only 38,000 industrial robots annually, leaving 90% of factories untouched.
item.content:encoded:
When Tutor pitches to first-time robot buyers, it never mentions models or AI—just one number: $16 an hour. The strategy reflects a vast market gap: America deploys only 38,000 industrial robots annually, leaving 90% of factories untouched.

From a company that has actually shipped robots to hundreds of factories. Unlike most robotics startups, it focuses on hardware, sales cycles, and supply chains—not model innovation.

3:13 Start with robot deployment, not model training
Josh observes that 99% of robotics startups begin with a model or data insight, but few ask what a robot actually needs to do. Tutor inverts this. Even if perfect software could connect 8 billion humans' physical intelligence to any machine, robots still wouldn't exist, supply chains wouldn't exist, and customers wouldn't exist—because robotics remains a cottage industry even in manufacturing and logistics. So Tutor deploys robots in the real world first, then builds datasets, models, and supply chains from that experience.

9:27 There's no internet for physical labor, so build one
Josh explains the company name by contrasting social media and email—natural human behaviors that inadvertently created a training dataset for LLMs—with physical work, which leaves no digital record. When Josh picks up his coffee cup, no one records the pressure or angle his fingers used. Tutor's solution isn't to invent physical reasoning from scratch. Instead, it deploys robots into the real world where human remote operators (the "tutors") teach machines new tasks. This amounts to building an internet for robot training data, and the process itself generates economic value by making customer goods cheaper.

16:47 America deployed 38,000 industrial robots last year. That's it.
Josh offers a sobering comparison: U.S. factories and warehouses took delivery of just 38,000 industrial robots in 2025—a volume so small that even one successful humanoid robot model would barely register statistically. The problem runs deeper than quantity. Robotics OEMs like Fanuc and ABB make machines either overseas or for systems integrators handling fast-repeat tasks—not designed around the choices needed to work with advanced LLMs. Tutor had no choice but to design and manufacture its own hardware rather than source off the shelf.

18:54 Two robots handle 80–90% of warehouse and factory jobs
Tutor makes only two models. Cassie is a single-arm robot with a suction gripper—a "workhorse" powered by a foundation model with 200M–400M parameters. It handles heavy pallets and cartons, solving the labor problem of turnover (workers average 55 years old and quit within three months). Sunny is a wheeled (not legged, because factory floors are polished) industrial humanoid robot engineered to run continuously for three to ten years at human speed and reliability, with industrial-grade collaborative safety. Josh claims these two robots cover 80 to 90 percent of manufacturing and logistics work.

23:58 The sales call opens with an hourly rate, not a model
Tutor's customers are almost entirely first-time robot buyers—people familiar with older automation who assume robots can't apply to their business. Breaking through means abandoning the pitch about AI, models, or tutors. Instead, Tutor calls and asks, "Have you considered a robot at $16 an hour?"—a proposition they've never heard. This alignment of incentives lets Tutor move multiples faster than traditional industrial automation. First call to signature: 40–60 days. Signature to robot running on site: roughly 40 days. Installation often happens in a day or even hours.

30:10 Betting on a big customer and custom work is how robot startups die
Josh has observed this pattern repeat five to ten times: a research-heavy robotics company lands an LOI from a large customer, spends two years building a hyper-customized system, and it either doesn't work or the customer's problem disappears. The company dies. His lesson: work with diverse small and medium customers. That constraint—far from being a weakness—forces the company to build a true general-purpose robotic body and platform, not a Rube Goldberg machine built for a single buyer.

32:16 Demand shifts entirely when factory-built homes undercut site-built by just 1 percent
Josh recalls an example from a Wisconsin housing factory worker: factory-built homes currently cost 5% more than site construction. But the instant factory construction becomes just 1% cheaper—even fractionally—developers will shift all demand to the factory model. He uses this to argue that robots don't unlock linearly declining costs. Cross a critical threshold and entire industries flip. The same logic applies to materials recovery at landfills and similar markets where cost inflection points trigger structural shifts in where work gets done.

39:20 China's bet on yesterday's automation may be a long-term miscalculation
When pressed on how robotics will reshape factory location and regional manufacturing patterns, Josh pivots to geopolitics. China invested heavily in the previous generation of industrial automation, and it paid off handsomely. But over the long term, it may be a massive mistake. The U.S. is now undertaking greenfield automation using general-purpose robots without tearing out old lines first—an advantage China lacks. Josh acknowledges that supply chains remain deeply linked: Chinese and American firms both invest in each other's markets and build their own capabilities. Tutor itself is moving more component supply vertically back to its Watertown factory because the company has become one of the largest demand sources for certain OEMs.

item.title: Two traders cornered the onion market and forced Congress to permanently ban onion futures
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-02-stuffmissed-两个农民囤光洋葱操纵期货-让国会专门立法禁掉了洋葱期货/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-02-stuffmissed-两个农民囤光洋葱操纵期货-让国会专门立法禁掉了洋葱期货/
item.category: Stuff You Missed in History Class
item.description: The two conspired to buy nearly all Chicago onions, forced distributors to sign a secret deal, then shorted the market and crashed prices to historic lows, leading Congress to permanently ban onion futures trading.
item.content:encoded:
The two conspired to buy nearly all Chicago onions, forced distributors to sign a secret deal, then shorted the market and crashed prices to historic lows, leading Congress to permanently ban onion futures trading.

The story itself is absurd, but the real lesson is this: proving market manipulation intent is harder in court than proving the harm it caused.

4:04 Futures were supposed to stabilize prices, but the data didn't support it
The classic justification for futures trading is that it lets farmers and wholesalers lock in prices early, making markets more stable and prices less volatile. But the show cites a 1956 Commodity Exchange Authority report showing that from 1929 to 1956, onion prices actually swung wider than many other commodities with futures markets. The stabilizing effect futures were supposed to provide never materialized for onions.

13:24 The two conspired to corner nearly all Chicago onions
Vince Kasuga, a floor trader with onion-farming roots, and Sam Siegel, an exchange member, quietly bought 928 November onion futures contracts in late 1955, accounting for 45% of that month's open interest. When the contracts settled on November 30, Kasuga alone held 262 railcars of onions—over 7.8 million pounds—half of Chicago's entire onion supply. Including outstanding contracts, by early 1956 the two controlled roughly 1,000 railcars, nearly equal to Chicago's entire cash onion supply.

16:28 They pressured distributors into a secret deal
Kasuga and Siegel didn't stop at hoarding. They approached 13 onion distributors in Chicago and threatened to dump their entire stockpile on the market—crushing everyone's prices—unless the distributors bought onions from them at their set price. The distributors eventually agreed to purchase 287 railcars for $1.60 per bag, totaling $275,000, with the condition that Kasuga and Siegel would not make any additional deliveries for the rest of the season. Both sides understood the deal had to remain secret.

18:34 After the deal fell apart, they shorted the market
In January and February 1956, distributors began suspecting Kasuga and Siegel had reneged on their promise. All but one refused further payments or deliveries. The two then secretly shorted March onion futures, selling 858 railcars—44.3% of that month's open interest. They were the only ones holding short positions; everyone else was long. Distributor Dave Slinger later testified that Kasuga even called him urging him to short as well, saying the market would collapse to 50 cents in minutes if they all acted together.

21:37 Onion prices hit historic lows—the sack cost more than the onions
When the March 1956 futures settled, the market was flooded with onions. Prices plummeted to as low as 10 cents, closing at 15 cents—an all-time low for the exchange, beating the previous record of 43 cents. According to Kasuga's nephew in an NPR interview, a mesh sack for onions cost 20 cents to make, yet a full sack sold for only 10 cents. The show notes this crash wasn't purely artificial—Texas onions unexpectedly harvested early that same period, which also drove the collapse.

26:43 Intent is harder to prove than harm
The Commodity Exchange Authority's hearing found that Kasuga and Siegel's December 1955 coercion of distributors and March 1956 short-selling to suppress prices both constituted illegal market manipulation, even though they claimed they only wanted to stabilize prices. But regarding their massive November futures purchases, the ruling acknowledged that manipulation was common on the onion exchange and ultimately found insufficient evidence of manipulative intent—that charge was dropped. The line between legal trading and manipulation can be blurry.

27:44 Congress directly prohibited onion futures despite existing market manipulation laws
After the 1960 ruling, Kasuga, Siegel, and National Produce Distributors were barred from all futures markets for 10 months. But the bigger consequence came earlier: on August 28, 1958, a bill introduced by Representative Gerald Ford—pushed by affected Michigan onion farmers and signed by President Eisenhower—directly prohibited onion futures trading, even though market manipulation was already illegal under existing law. The Chicago Mercantile Exchange sued claiming it was unconstitutional; they lost and didn't appeal. The law remains in effect today.

31:49 Movie futures: the only other commodity banned after onions
After the onion case, commodity futures saw another scandal in 1963: the soybean oil swindle. Tony DeAngelis substituted water for soybean oil, stockpiled it as collateral, and manipulated soybean futures, ultimately serving 10 years. Regulatively, Congress passed the Commodity Futures Trading Commission Act in 1974, and the Dodd-Frank Act addressed the 2008 crisis in 2010. But trying to legislatively ban a specific futures contract has succeeded only once since onions: the 2010 movie futures ban, prompted by the Motion Picture Association's lobbying. In the same law, onions and movie box office remain the only two commodities explicitly prohibited from futures trading.

item.title: Scientists tricked a rat's brain into thinking salt water tasted good
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-02-mindscape-科学家让大鼠的大脑-骗-自己盐水很好喝/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-02-mindscape-科学家让大鼠的大脑-骗-自己盐水很好喝/
item.description: Researchers used optogenetics to amplify reward-signal neurons in rat brains so that when the rat drank salt water it hated, the brain still judged 'this was good'—sensory input and reward signals can be directly severed.
item.content:encoded:
Researchers used optogenetics to amplify reward-signal neurons in rat brains so that when the rat drank salt water it hated, the brain still judged 'this was good'—sensory input and reward signals can be directly severed.

The content spans behavioral game theory experiments, brain imaging research, and optogenetic manipulation, with high information density and little filler, though the second half leans into neuroscience details.

3:45 Rationality is economics' limiting case, not how humans actually decide
Camerer describes the utility-maximization model as a ‘limiting case’ in economic theory, like a simplifying assumption in physics—expert tasters with extensive experience who can rank all options might approach perfect rationality, but that is not the state of most people most of the time. The model resembles the endpoint of learning rather than its starting point. Textbook ‘rational actors’ were never what the field actually believed; they were just a convenient launching point.

12:14 Life and death probability questions should add to 100%—they don't
When asked ‘what is the probability you'll live to 75,’ people answer with a number like 90%. But when asked separately ‘what is the probability you'll die before 75,’ the answer will not be 10%—the two should sum to 100%, but they do not. Camerer's collaborator Eric Johnson attributes this to ‘default endorsement bias’: the question frames attention toward survival or death accordingly. Frame effects are not trivial—salad dressing labeled ‘10% fat’ sells differently from ‘90% fat-free’. Advertisers and political consultants have long understood this.

15:02 Chess masters guess numbers like everyone else in this game
In the guessing game where players choose 0–100 and the closest guess to two-thirds of the average wins, most people reason only one or two steps deep—‘others will guess 50, so I'll guess 33; or others will guess 33, so I'll guess 22’—and almost no one reasons all the way to zero. The New York Times ran this with 50,000 players; the data shows 33 appears far more often than 22, and deeper reasoning is nearly nonexistent. Surprisingly, professional chess players perform about the same as amateurs in this game—deep strategic thinking appears to be highly domain-specific and does not transfer across domains.

29:55 Audiences can't reverse-engineer ‘no reviews’ as a bad signal
From 600 major theatrical releases (2000–2009), roughly 10% are ‘cold opens’—studios don't send films to critics beforehand. These films later show the lowest aggregate critic scores, indicating studios knew they had lemons and held them back. But the cognitive hierarchy model predicts that some viewers will read ‘no reviews’ as neutral rather than bad, like Sherlock Holmes' dog that did not bark—most people won't reverse-engineer ‘why isn't anyone reviewing this?’. Because of this reasoning gap, cold-open films outperform their true quality by roughly 15% at the box office.

40:19 Neuroeconomics began with a silent room of economists
In 1997 Camerer and George Loewenstein organized a conference in Pittsburgh bringing together economists and neuroscientists to explore whether economic questions could be studied with neuroscience methods. Most economists stayed silent throughout—in the field, admitting ignorance carries low status. Notably, Peter Diamond, Al Roth, and Paul Romer were all in that room and later won the Nobel Prize, yet except for Romer's one paper on emotion, virtually none pursued this direction. Neuroeconomics actually advanced only when Caltech acquired an unused brain scanner and a few professors were willing to bet their tenure on it.

52:11 People who think one step deeper activate stronger mentalizing circuits
In the guessing game, players who reason forward—choosing 22 instead of 33—show stronger activity in brain regions responsible for ‘mentalizing,’ understanding others' thoughts: the right temporoparietal junction and dorsomedial prefrontal cortex. The test works by showing subjects the same photograph twice, once asking ‘what is this person doing’ and once asking ‘why is this person doing that’; the activation difference in the second version indexes mentalizing. Camerer acknowledges research here is sparse, but existing studies point the same direction: strategic depth and mentalizing circuitry use are linked.

1:00:29 Gym check-in intervals form a nearly perfect power law
Analyzing gym attendance data from roughly 20,000 people over 1,500 days, Camerer plotted visit intervals—many short gaps, many long gaps, no bell curve—and on a log-log graph it traces almost a perfect line (R²=0.97), a ‘burstiness’ that should be extremely rare in social science data. He later discovered mathematicians proved in 1954 that non-FIFO queuing, where ‘priority queue’ admits some people ahead of order, produces power-law distributions; such results appear mostly in physics journals. Their ‘Neural Autopilot’ model—habit-driven decision-making tracking only two values, the last choice and reward reliability—reproduces this effect with a slope of roughly -2.

1:20:23 Light can make rat brains misread foul tastes as rewards
The brain contains neurons encoding ‘reward prediction error’, discovered in 1997 by Schultz, Dayan, and Montague in rodents. Using optogenetics, Camerer's team amplified these neurons when a rat pressed a lever and drank salt water it hated, creating artificial ‘this was good’ signals in the brain—the rat kept pressing despite its facial expressions and behavior showing it disliked the taste. Camerer calls this ‘neural gaslighting’: the sensory system knows the truth, but the hijacked reward signal drowns it out.

item.title: The $300 billion structured notes market is quietly amplifying US stock declines
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-02-oddlots-3000亿美元结构票据市场-正在悄悄放大美股下跌的力道/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-02-oddlots-3000亿美元结构票据市场-正在悄悄放大美股下跌的力道/
item.description: When worst-of auto-callable notes linked to the S&P, Nasdaq, and Russell indexes stop knocking out on schedule, dealers are forced to dump volatility exposure simultaneously, just as market-makers willing to buy it back are shrinking.
item.content:encoded:
When worst-of auto-callable notes linked to the S&P, Nasdaq, and Russell indexes stop knocking out on schedule, dealers are forced to dump volatility exposure simultaneously, just as market-makers willing to buy it back are shrinking.

Greeks-heavy but explains why structured notes' slow decay hurts markets more than sharp crashes; challenging but substantive.

1:04 Structured notes are a hidden technical current in the market
The episode opens by positioning structured notes as a technical flow separate from fundamental narratives—whether AI stocks should rise is one question, but what actually drives near-term prices is the forced hedging action when derivatives positions like structured notes expire or knock out. The hosts mention Nvidia's credit default swaps recently ticked slightly higher, a sign of market ‘high-frequency tremors’; this is why they dedicated an entire episode to structured notes.

3:05 Essentially, a child of bank deposits and derivatives
Alex defines it this way: you give the issuer your money, forgo interest, and take on their credit risk; the bank then uses the ‘forgone interest’ to buy and sell options, customizing the return shape you want—bullish participation, downside protection, or the more common ‘yield’ structure, where the bank sells you a put option and wraps the premium into coupon payments. Three approaches can be freely combined; the bank is like a chef, cutting the same option ingredients into different products for different clients.

8:15 US structured notes hit $300 billion this year
SEC-registered structured notes in the US are on track to reach roughly $300 billion in issuance this year, versus about $200 billion last year. The fastest-growing category is worst-of auto-callable notes linked to the S&P, Nasdaq, and Russell indexes. The reason: Russell has basically flatlined for years, but since last year's ‘liberation day’ it's been climbing, causing notes that should have knocked out repeatedly to keep extending, their size rolling larger.

21:50 Falling markets force dealers to dump volatility exposure all at once
When markets climb early in the year, notes knock out frequently and roll forward; dealers' hedge positions self-clear in a virtuous cycle. But once markets turn down, notes that fail to knock out start piling up, dealers' vega exposure (sensitivity to implied volatility) balloons, and just then the off-market counterparties who had been hedging pull back because their own portfolios are shrinking—fewer buyers step up. This is the ‘spot up, vol up’ pattern Charlie McElligot and Nomura colleagues observe playing out in the structured notes market.

26:55 Single-stock notes use daily observation, flipping exposure on and off
Tickets linked to individual stocks pursue higher coupons by adding ‘conditional coupons’ (skip payment if the stock falls too far) and daily-observation knockout features, letting the product terminate almost any day after an observation window. The result is that banks' risk exposure becomes extremely binary: once a stock bounces, knockout fires instantly, vega erases; once it falls, the bank instantly holds a full short put position. Markets thus see a ‘either have vega or have none’ on-off pattern instead of smooth change.

38:06 Two-year notes can be forced to extend to five
Worst-of notes typical in US markets carry nominal 3-to-5-year terms but dealers hedge on a 2-year expected life. Once indexes fall and notes refuse to knock out, actual duration can stretch to five years; dealers' hedges, built for 2 years, suddenly have to cover an extra three years of vega exposure. Conversely, if an index then rallies back near all-time highs, dealers find they still hold 5-year hedge shorts, but the note knocked out in three months—this structure is called ‘peak vega’ internally.

44:17 One stock's early surge knocks out entire basket notes instantly
Alex highlights what he calls the most creative design: a three-stock basket note where if any one stock rises 20% on day one, no matter how the other two perform, the product knocks out immediately. If the leader then crashes while the note already knocked out, that deep-in-the-money put position evaporates—the bank thus holds a position extremely sensitive to ‘vol of vol’ (volatility of volatility): the moment all three stocks rise, risk disappears; the moment one lags, the bank faces a major short put that can vanish any time.

45:20 2018's lessons spawned a new generation of product designs
Alex notes that innovation in structure often starts from real past losses. In 2018, a batch of dealers took heavy losses in ‘slow grinding down’ conditions—not a crash or a non-event, but a modest decline that never fully compressed, so hedges kept misfiring. The market then designed new-type notes to handle that middle ground—‘fall a little but not through, knock out even if stopping in a zone’—but new designs bring new second-order problems.

item.title: Airbnb survived because its business model was strong enough to mask management chaos
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-02-howibuilt-airbnb能活下来-是因为商业模式好到掩盖了管理混乱/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-02-howibuilt-airbnb能活下来-是因为商业模式好到掩盖了管理混乱/
item.description: He argues that Airbnb's strong business model masked management chaos until the pandemic forced a crisis that pushed him from delegation to hands-on founder mode.
item.content:encoded:
He argues that Airbnb's strong business model masked management chaos until the pandemic forced a crisis that pushed him from delegation to hands-on founder mode.

Listen to someone who admits ‘I'm a great founder, a terrible CEO’ explain why delegation becomes a death sentence in early-stage companies.

3:14 Billion-dollar success cannot heal the need for validation
On Airbnb's IPO day at a valuation exceeding $100 billion, Chesky said the next day was one of the loneliest moments of his life. With no bell-ringing ceremony during the COVID lockdown, no celebration with family and friends, just Zoom boxes, he woke in pajamas to a regular meeting and realized his life hadn't actually changed. This exposed a long-standing truth: he'd been driven by a desperate need for recognition and feeling special, and reaching the top couldn't heal that wound.

11:28 Great founder instincts completely fail in the CEO role
Chesky says he was born to be a founder—since childhood assembling and disassembling Christmas toys, selling things to friends—he'd been training for 20 years. But the CEO job is counterintuitive: the common advice of hiring great people, trusting them fully, and hands-off management works for mature companies but is a death sentence for early-stage ones. What actually works is hiring people just slightly ahead of you, people you must follow closely.

16:39 Avoiding difficult conversations sabotaged the entire team
He admits he was deeply conflict-averse; when someone wasn't performing, he wouldn't act on it, even doing their work for them. This both hid the problem and robbed the person of the chance to grow. Someone later told him that baseball players don't take themselves out of the game—most underperformers think they're doing fine. The responsibility to replace someone always falls on the CEO, not on the person to step aside.

23:54 CEO isolation is like being principal of your own high school
He compares becoming CEO to being told you're now principal of your own high school—employees stop being friends; everyone looks wary when you walk into the room. He wrote to Obama for help. The response: you're lonely. Humans need solitude, close family, a dozen friends to confide in, a community of hundreds, and a larger world—concentric circles. He realized he'd broken the connection at almost every level.

36:20 Runaway early success made him overconfident about everything
Airbnb exploded in 18 months, and that easy ride bred arrogance—the team thought any new business would be just as simple. So they expanded crazily and hired without laying the foundation or proper structure. The real problem wasn't money or resources; it was that the business model was so strong it masked management mistakes. Like eBay coasting on a good model but getting outrun by Amazon, which had stronger execution and thinner margins.

40:29 Pandemic crisis forced delegation to become deep hands-on involvement
When the pandemic wiped out 80% of business in 8 weeks, it shifted from nice-to-have crisis management to a matter of survival. For the first time, he truly went deep into the details. He started skipping levels to meet with frontline executors instead of just hearing from executives. He summarized this as empowerment, not autonomy—subordinates can autonomously decide how to do things, but not which direction to go. Without that, everyone walks their own path.

49:45 Switching to founder mode: nearly the entire exec team quit
When he decided to stop being hands-off and dive into details, nearly the entire original executive team eventually left. His response wasn't to convince everyone to stay, but to keep just ten core executives willing to work this way. He let results speak—outcomes already validated during the crisis. He deliberately hired from people who'd worked under Bezos and Jobs, since they already understood this management style.

1:03:10 Using the company's core strength: free housing for disaster survivors
Starting with Hurricane Sandy in 2012, Airbnb has provided free stays for Afghan refugees, Ukrainian refugees, and LA wildfire survivors. The non-profit airbnb.org responds to a disaster roughly every other day on average. The plan now: invest $500 million to provide one million free nights per year over the next five years, aiming to become one of the world's largest free housing providers.

item.title: AI inference no longer commands 90% margins; each supply layer takes 20-30%
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-02-twentyvc-ai推理不再有90-毛利-每多一层供应商就分走利润/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-02-twentyvc-ai推理不再有90-毛利-每多一层供应商就分走利润/
item.description: A dollar from customer to Nvidia passes through applications, models, infrastructure, and cloud. Each layer takes 20–30% margin. This is why AI infrastructure companies can't return to software's golden-age profitability.
item.content:encoded:
A dollar from customer to Nvidia passes through applications, models, infrastructure, and cloud. Each layer takes 20–30% margin. This is why AI infrastructure companies can't return to software's golden-age profitability.

Modal just reached a $15.75 billion valuation, and the CEO rarely speaks with such candor about the realities of GPU procurement, capital allocation missteps, and the true limits of post-training. Information density exceeds typical founder interviews.

9:09 Capital is not a moat; buying GPU is real cash burn
Modal is profitable on P&L but cash-flow negative—the company burns through cash to secure GPU capacity. This contrasts with Modal's early days, when capital efficiency was extreme (only a few hundred million per month). The shift began a year ago as GPU procurement and capacity-building dominated spending. Erik resists calling capital a moat (the term is overused), but admits it does help at this stage. He also warns that VCs push more capital into companies than they need, causing unnecessary dilution. Early-stage companies should stay lean, take less money, and keep VCs hungry for the next round.

13:09 Selling tokens alone dooms you to a price war
Pure inference has no moat. If you're just converting tokens to dollars, customers have zero switching costs, triggering a race to the bottom. Modal spent five years layering post-training, sandboxes, agent infrastructure, low-latency and batch inference into one complete toolkit—not a single product. The goal: customers buy a full toolbox, not a single-trick pony. The complexity of infrastructure itself becomes the real, hard-to-copy moat.

15:13 The 90% software margin era is over; stack complexity ensures it
This is an underappreciated structural fact about the inference market. Every dollar flowing from customer to Nvidia traverses a full stack: applications, models, infrastructure, cloud, and chip vendors. Each layer takes 20–30% margin. No company maintains 90% margins anymore. Modal's long-term margin expectation is 40–60%, with no path back to traditional software profitability.

17:16 GPU procurement looks like an open drug market
Erik describes his GTC experience: running between 500 different cloud vendors asking whether they have GPU inventory. He likens the scene to an outdoor drug market, except the product is compute. Modal now works with 25 NeoCloud providers and controls roughly 0.1% of global compute. The long-term play: as Modal controls more GPUs, it can aggregate thousands of customers' fluctuating, unpredictable demand into a smooth curve, then match supply efficiently—a capability Erik believes no one else can replicate.

34:35 Sandboxes had a four-year cold start before revenue exploded
Modal launched its sandbox product in 2023. For two years it barely registered. Then summer 2025 arrived—models suddenly got good at code generation and building complete applications—and sandboxes went from zero to $300 million annualized revenue, now roughly one-third of Modal's total. This illustrates an infrastructure pattern: you can't predict which building block becomes a hit. Stable Diffusion and ChatGPT were not foreseen when serverless functions were being built. The only move is to lay good foundational pieces and wait for timing to align.

36:36 DeepSeek made Modal see it had bet on the wrong resource
Modal started late on LLM inference. The team assumed it would be a pure commodity race to the bottom, so it didn't push hard. After DeepSeek's release, the team realized it had to move fast. In one year, it expanded the LLM inference team from one or two people to 30 and is now a top-three provider of open-source LLM inference. When asked whether open-source inference has peaked and frontier models will rebound, Erik disagrees. He rejects the framing—it treats the market as a fixed pie. His view: open-source and frontier inference will each grow 5–20x over the next few years. These are not zero-sum.

41:41 Reinforcement learning only works on short-feedback tasks
Here is the boundary of post-training: RL works in coding, network security, and mathematics (with Lean) because they have verifiable, limited feedback loops—code runs in a sandbox and produces a testable result. Whether this scales to longer-feedback cycles is unclear. Software engineers' work has a slower feedback loop, so this part of the job won't be automated soon. That said, Erik has been wrong on predictions like this many times. He expects that work completable within 24 hours or a week will be fully automated, but longer cycles remain safe—for now.

45:49 Selling data to frontier labs is the most profitable business today
Asked what he'd do at age 20 again, Erik says: start a data environment company selling to frontier labs, especially code environments. The money in this space is ‘almost unbelievable’. Caveat: such companies have excellent cash flow today, but whether they support a durable venture-scale business is an open question. His advice: ‘take the money regardless. It's a good business’.

item.title: Peter the Great Returns: The Ships He Took, the Parliaments He Left
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-02-historyhit-彼得大帝西游归来-只搬技术-绝口不提议会与自由/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-02-historyhit-彼得大帝西游归来-只搬技术-绝口不提议会与自由/
item.description: He visited post-Glorious Revolution England and the Dutch Republic, but brought home only shipbuilding technique, shaving ordinances, and gun-fort blueprints—parliament and political freedom stayed in Western Europe.
item.content:encoded:
He visited post-Glorious Revolution England and the Dutch Republic, but brought home only shipbuilding technique, shaving ordinances, and gun-fort blueprints—parliament and political freedom stayed in Western Europe.

The guest is a scholar of Russian society and criminal history. She moves from witnessing a coup at age ten through her subject's beatings of his own son, placing "greatness" and "bloodlust" in the same body with granular detail.

2:00 The embassy demolished England's most famous hedge garden
Peter's mission lodged at John Evelyn's Deptford estate, site of a 400-foot holly hedge—9 feet high, 5 feet thick—that Samuel Pepys called ‘one of the finest things I have ever seen in my life’. Visitors discovered wheelbarrows and treated them as toys, pushing each other through the hedge until it was leveled. They used portraits as targets and chopped furniture for firewood. Historians call it a rock band in a resort—and the 6-foot-8, 25-year-old tsar led the charge.

10:21 A ten-year-old boy watched relatives impaled on palace pikes
In 1682, the death of Tsar Feodor III triggered succession chaos. The Streltsi, hereditary musketeers, rebelled against young Peter's claim. The ten-year-old hid behind his mother while relatives were thrown from the Kremlin walls onto Streltsi pikes below. A regency agreement—Peter and his half-brother Ivan V with half-sister Sophia as regent—ended the immediate crisis. The trauma left him permanently unwilling to tolerate any rival's threat to his life.

15:35 The embassy called itself alliance-building; it was really a fact-finding mission
Officially, Peter sought an anti-Ottoman coalition among Northern European powers. The guest stresses that what he actually wanted was to learn what the West could teach. This was not worship of the West but transaction: ships that sail, cannons that fire, fortresses that hold. Over roughly 18 months (1697–1698), he concentrated on Holland and England, with stops in German principalities and Vienna. He wanted knowledge, ideas, and talent moved back to Russia, not Western institutions copied.

24:52 He ordered beards shaved, then forbade any talk of parliaments
Back home, Peter launched a cultural revolution: mandatory shaving for nobles (beards showed God's image in Orthodox theology—a raw religious nerve), women in public society, simplified alphabet for secular printing, Julian calendar and January 1 as New Year. But his hosts had been post-Glorious Revolution England and a Dutch republic. He came home indifferent to political freedom, constitutionalism. This was not model-copying. It was pure selection: a few frigates, a few beards—but absolutely no parliament.

28:12 He lost catastrophically at Narva, then won because his opponent looked away
In 1700, opening battle of the Great Northern War: the Russian army was annihilated by King Charles XII of Sweden. All artillery and supplies captured. Total humiliation. Peter's fortune was that Charles XII turned to the Polish battlefield to the west. That window let Peter rebuild his army and start a navy. The war lasted 1700–1721 and became the shadow across his entire reign—most of his reforms were rushed through to serve it.

30:18 Saint Petersburg was built by conscripting thousands into a swamp
In 1703, Peter built Saint Petersburg at the mouth of the Neva to project power into the Baltic. It began as a military fortress and became Russia's new capital (formally, 1710). It rose because Peter could summon thousands of forced laborers to dig canals and build palaces in a mosquito-infested swamp, and order his own nobles to move there. The guest emphasizes: not a city grown from voluntary settlement and commerce, but the direct projection of one man's autocratic will.

41:42 The tsar who beat his own son to death with a whip
Peter and his eldest son Alexei had an irreconcilable break. Alexei fled to Habsburg protection. Peter saw betrayal and feared that nobles opposed to his reforms would rally to Alexei as a banner. He lured Alexei back to Saint Petersburg, charged him with treason, and beat him with a knout—a raw leather whip that kills in a few blows. Alexei died from torture in 1718. The guest sees the tangle: real succession politics and the 1682 Streltsi wound. Peter increasingly saw anyone pulling Russia in a different direction as a traitor.

45:49 The nobles spoke French; the peasants' life barely changed except they got poorer
Peter left an autocratic state perfected: the poll tax bound peasants to the land because landowners and officials now profited from keeping them there. Serfdom hardened. Church and nobility—potential checks on tsarist power—became state appendages. The nobility, meanwhile, Westernized: by the 1750s, they spoke French. Peasant life stayed nearly unchanged except taxes climbed and military service stretched longer. Alexander Herzen later called this ‘two Russias’. In the 19th century, Peter's legacy was always contested—some called him the man who turned Russia westward, others the man who tore indigenous Russian culture apart. That argument has never ended.

item.title: ADHD is not a self-control deficit, but a different way the nervous system processes the world
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-02-parentmojo-adhd不是自控力缺陷-而是神经系统处理世界的方式不同/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-02-parentmojo-adhd不是自控力缺陷-而是神经系统处理世界的方式不同/
item.description: Mainstream frameworks treat ADHD as an executive function deficit correctable through self-control; this counselor argues the root is inborn differences in attention regulation and sensory processing, traits that once were survival advantages for humans.
item.content:encoded:
Mainstream frameworks treat ADHD as an executive function deficit correctable through self-control; this counselor argues the root is inborn differences in attention regulation and sensory processing, traits that once were survival advantages for humans.

Directly challenges the most authoritative medical framework in ADHD discourse with specific counterexamples and evidence, rather than vague contrarianism.

5:04 Attention regulation, not executive function, is the root problem
The mainstream account traces ADHD to executive-function deficits, but B. Lourenco asks: why would executive function fail? She locates it instead in attention-regulation differences—not deficits but different regulation. The mechanism is sensory variation: the world is noisier, more intense, harder to screen out for ADHD brains. One theory she cites: ADHD may stem from early hunter-gatherer neurology, hence an interest-based nervous system—not a switch to do what you should, but constant alertness to what is that? because it could mean food or survival.

10:23 The lifespan gap is real, but the explanation is oversimplified
B. Lourenco acknowledges the data—ADHD people do have worse health outcomes and shorter lifespans—but rejects the pure impulse-control story. By that logic, living longer just means controlling yourself better, which doesn't hold. She points out that the medical model omits the comorbidities common in ADHD: mast cell activation syndrome (MCAS), Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, fibromyalgia. Those diseases themselves shorten life. If doctors fixate on impulse control, a patient with these comorbidities gets told to manage themselves, not screened for other conditions.

13:37 ADHD requires structure and design, not control as the answer
Against objections like "rules help everyone" (traffic laws), B. Lourenco draws a line between structure and control. ADHD does need structure and constraint—free-form chaos won't work for this nervous system. But treating control as the only answer is broken: it puts all burden on the ADHD person or parent, not the environment. It reinforces "if you wanted to, you could," which isn't true. There is an impulse-control piece, she allows, but the answer isn't more control. It's finding structures people actually adopt and stick with.

16:27 One household, two divergent medication histories
B. Lourenco has a child who was diagnosed and medicated for ADHD from childhood; she herself wasn't identified until adulthood. This split explains why she and the other parent clash on drugs. She tells listeners with similar childhood-medication histories: the problem wasn't just "too many kids on meds"—it was how much each kid took and that no one heard their voice. Those two wrongs—overdosing and silencing—can be separated; her child's path doesn't have to repeat them.

17:24 Whether children should have a right to refuse medication: they clash
The episode mentions ADHD authority Barkley's stance: prefrontal development is incomplete, so kids lack the capacity to decide; medication is 100 percent a parent call, kids' input irrelevant. B. Lourenco calls this infantilizing, a denial of the child's autonomy as a whole person. She allows that medication works fast and gets picked first for that reason—environmental change takes upkeep—but speed alone shouldn't make it eternal or primary. Drugs can be a starting point, not the only or forever top option.

19:41 One needs quiet, one craves noise: neither is wrong
When a parent desires calm but the child is wired for novelty and stimulation, B. Lourenco's first step: name it. Sensory need isn't chosen; it just is. This doesn't make anyone bad. But within the parent-child bond, the power is asymmetric. Parents bring more self-regulation skills and carry more load—a ratio that shifts with age. A four- to six-year-old can already understand "Mom needs quiet for a few minutes." B. Lourenco tells her kids she's taking a break and will be back—this normalizes her need and teaches them "Mom is a separate person from me."

23:48 Stop blaming yourself first; then find people who can hold you
Asked what to say to newly diagnosed or questioning parents, B. Lourenco offers two things. First: stop shaming and blaming yourself. Put ADHD on the human timeline—it's not a fundamental error. Diversity itself is why the human species endured. Second: build a real, shame-free, non-judgmental network. Call someone trusted and say "I'm about to break, give me ten minutes"; have them supervise the kid even by phone, or video-link a distant friend to watch for a while. Needing help doesn't mean you're broken; it means you're human.

26:28 Should society change for 5 percent of people
Jen closes with a memory: Barkley was asked, "Do we really reshape the whole society for 5 percent of the population?" His answer was a cold, scornful "No." Jen's is the opposite: yes—because designs that serve a marginalized group usually make life smoother for everyone. A routine that helps an ADHD kid get out the door on time usually helps the whole family's morning flow.

item.title: What ignited Hungary's 1956 revolution was a debate club run by poets and writers
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-02-restishistory-点燃匈牙利1956年革命的-是一群诗人作家办的辩论俱乐部/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-02-restishistory-点燃匈牙利1956年革命的-是一群诗人作家办的辩论俱乐部/
item.description: After eleven years of authoritarian rule, the uprising was ignited not by underground movements or worker leaders, but by a public debate organized by poets and writers—showing that the Rakosi regime had nothing left but force, no hearts to win.
item.content:encoded:
After eleven years of authoritarian rule, the uprising was ignited not by underground movements or worker leaders, but by a public debate organized by poets and writers—showing that the Rakosi regime had nothing left but force, no hearts to win.

It fully reconstructs how Hungary's eleven years of authoritarian rule spiraled step by step, and clearly explains the causal chain from the Rakosi regime's collapse to the uprising.

12:12 Hungary's postwar collapse produced the worst hyperinflation in recorded history
As Nazi Germany's ally, Hungary was occupied by the Red Army after the war and received no Western sympathy—Stalin could do as he pleased. The war claimed roughly one in ten of the population (about 1 million people), and 500,000 were captured into Soviet POW camps. Over half the nation's factories, railways, and livestock were destroyed. The resulting economic collapse produced humanity's most severe hyperinflation on record in 1946, as currency lost all meaning—this was the backdrop that made Hungarians willing to accept any ‘order’.

15:22 The Communist Party used salami tactics to monopolize power over four years
In the November 1945 election, Communists won just 17% of the vote, far behind the agrarian Small Farmers' Party, the largest. But their strategy required controlling only one ministry—the Interior, which meant the police—plus the Red Army's ability to adjudicate any dispute. This was enough to systematically consume the power of rival parties. Rakosi himself called it ‘Salami politics’: slice by slice, seize a ministry, purge a group, until one day the whole salami falls into your hand. By 1949, Hungary had only one legal political party.

22:40 Rakosi's regime charged 750,000 with treason, executed 2,000, imprisoned 200,000
To wrench Hungary from peasant agriculture into heavy industry, Rakosi spent almost nothing on consumer goods—no bread or meat in shops, clothes impossible to fit, workers rising at 4:30 a.m. and forced into political study sessions until 10 p.m. after their shifts. According to British ambassador Brian Cartledge in his history of Hungary, from 1949 to 1953 in a nation of 9-10 million, 750,000 were charged with ‘endangering the state,’ 2,000 were executed, and 200,000 were imprisoned, detained, or sentenced to hard labor. Children from bourgeois families were barred from university.

33:06 Khrushchev's secret denunciation of Stalin made Rakosi's regime ideologically indefensible
At the 20th Party Congress in February 1956, Khrushchev delivered an hours-long closed-door ‘secret report’ portraying Stalin as paranoid, bloodthirsty, and addicted to personality cults—a tyrant. Rakosi, the self-proclaimed ‘Stalin's best student,’ reeled as if struck by lightning. He told the Soviet ambassador, ‘What you did at the 20th Congress is a catastrophe,’ and tried to suppress the report's circulation in Hungary, issuing a ‘sanitized’ version the public mocked as childish. It backfired: by spring 1956, even party members dared call him ‘bald murderer’ in public, and when a history teacher spoke against him in class, no arrest followed.

40:26 Intellectuals, not revolutionaries, delivered the first blow to Rakosi's authority
The force that toppled Rakosi was not an underground network or worker cadre but the Petofi Circle, a Budapest salon originally devoted to literature. In June 1956, a debate on socialism drew over a thousand people. Yulia, widow of Rajk—the executed former security chief, herself newly released from prison—took the stage to accuse Rakosi of ‘murdering Rajk and trampling the honesty of this entire nation.’ The crowd surged with emotion. The next debate had to move to a larger venue; 6,000 more listened outside by loudspeaker. When Rakosi tried to suppress it in his old way—drawing up 400 people for trial—his own colleagues reported him to the Soviet ambassador instead. Within weeks, Moscow removed him and exiled him to Kyrgyzstan.

1:01:20 Students drafted a sixteen-point manifesto demanding elections and Soviet withdrawal
On October 20, students at universities in Szeged, the southern city, broke from the official Communist Youth League and formed their own organization. On the 22nd, a student assembly at Budapest Technical University—ironically convened by Communist student officials to ‘control the situation’—spiraled entirely out of control. Over 5,000 students crowded in and voted to follow Szeged's lead. Overnight they ran off a ‘16-point’ declaration, demanding the Stalin statue be torn down, the 1848 national emblem restored, free elections, Nagy as prime minister, and ‘immediate complete Soviet military withdrawal.’ They slipped leaflets onto trams and into factories, plastered them across the city—using the very methods of 1848's uprising.

1:05:26 Pulling down the Stalin statue transformed the uprising from patriotic to anti-Soviet
The march on October 23 began at the student monument in memorial spirit but swelled as workers and soldiers joined, the mood shifting from patriotic to anti-Soviet. Crowds began cutting the communist star from the flag's center and chanting ‘Russians go home.’ By evening, 200,000 packed Parliament Square. When Nagy took the microphone, he was booed off. Gero's radio address only inflamed tempers further, calling the protesters ‘bourgeois chauvinists and reactionaries.’ The crowd surged toward Heroes' Square. Workers wielding welding torches spent the night severing the massive Stalin statue at the ankles and hauling it away—leaving only a pair of copper boots, life-sized, standing on the pedestal.

1:12:39 Moscow debated intervention even as its own envoy reported the situation controlled
Late on October 23, Khrushchev convened an emergency Presidium session to debate intervention. Mikoyan and Defense Minister Zhukov counseled restraint: let Nagy manage it himself. ‘If we send in troops,’ they argued, ‘we'll only make things worse.’ Molotov led the hardliners, pressing for immediate suppression. Khrushchev sided with the hawks and ordered two divisions into Budapest, then two more from Romania. But Mikoyan, sent as a fact-finder, was cordoned off from the fighting and shown only what Hungarian officials wanted him to see. His report back to Moscow: ‘everything is under control.’ This reassurance would prove a pivotal miscalculation.

item.title: The Cuban Missile Crisis Almost Sparked Nuclear War—One Soviet Officer's Dissenting Vote Stopped It
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-02-empirehist-古巴导弹危机差点开打核战-全靠一名苏联军官投了反对票/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-02-empirehist-古巴导弹危机差点开打核战-全靠一名苏联军官投了反对票/
item.description: On Soviet nuclear submarine B-59, two of three officers agreed to launch a nuclear torpedo—only Arkhipov dissented, and his single vote held veto power under Soviet protocol, blocking nuclear war's trigger.
item.content:encoded:
On Soviet nuclear submarine B-59, two of three officers agreed to launch a nuclear torpedo—only Arkhipov dissented, and his single vote held veto power under Soviet protocol, blocking nuclear war's trigger.

The episode packs in dense detail—from televised debates to submarine nuclear-torpedo votes, all concrete scenes. It's perfect for systematically understanding the missile crisis decision-making chain, rather than just remembering the conclusion of "nearly war."

5:10 Television won the debate, but polling barely budged
The first televised presidential debate in American history drew 70 million viewers. The visual contrast was stark—Nixon looked haggard, his suit ill-fitting, unshaven with stubble prominent on camera; Kennedy appeared evenly tanned and composed. But Frederick cautions: if you read only the transcript, Nixon actually acquiesced to Kennedy multiple times and didn't lose as decisively as remembered. Television transformed the image of the presidency voters "saw," not the substance of the debate itself. After four debates, the race remained deadlocked; the TV effect has been somewhat magnified in hindsight.

14:32 Nixon publicly conceded, privately contested the outcome
Kennedy won with only 112,000 votes—one of America's closest presidential elections. Public memory casts Nixon as a statesman gracefully accepting defeat, telling reporters the nation couldn't withstand a constitutional crisis. But Frederick reveals that Republicans did mount vote-verification efforts in swing states like Illinois, Texas, and New Jersey; Nixon likely knew of and tacitly approved these, but ultimately didn't push the challenge to its conclusion.

26:09 The Bay of Pigs fiasco—Kennedy bore responsibility he couldn't shake
1,400 CIA-trained Cuban exiles landed at the Bay of Pigs; intelligence completely misjudged whether locals would rise up to help overthrow Castro. The operation failed catastrophically. Kennedy's defenders note he inherited the plan from Eisenhower and was pressed by the military and CIA to execute it. But Frederick notes Kennedy had advisors warning it was madness—he approved it anyway. What actually deserves credit: he refused the military's pleas to commit U.S. Air Force to salvage the operation, preventing further escalation.

32:39 Vienna summit: Khrushchev lectured Kennedy like a schoolmaster
Two months after the Bay of Pigs, Kennedy met Khrushchev in Vienna expecting rational negotiation with the Soviet leader. He'd prepared exhaustively, like cramming for an exam. But Khrushchev adopted an aggressively bullying posture, catching Kennedy off guard, leaving him outmatched in response. Even Kennedy admitted afterward his performance was poor. The backdrop: Khrushchev had preferred facing anyone but Nixon, and faced internal pressure from East German population flight. He used the meeting to test how much spine this young American president actually had.

38:51 In the missile crisis, he alone resisted the war room's military logic
U-2 reconnaissance photos showed Soviet missiles deployed in Cuba. Kennedy convened ExComm—the National Security Council's executive committee—to decide response. The crisis's first days saw Kennedy himself leaning toward military action; the military and most civilian advisors pushed hard for air strikes. But as discussion deepened, he pivoted. Any military action, in any form, carried too much risk. He shifted toward a political solution: a naval quarantine, not invasion. This stance was established early in the crisis, not a last-minute retreat forced by circumstances.

43:08 Two letters, one public and one secret—exchanged to end the crisis
Evening of October 26, Khrushchev sent an emotional letter proposing: if America pledged not to invade Cuba, Soviets would withdraw the missiles. Next morning came a second letter, more hardline, demanding America also remove its missiles from Turkey. Conventional wisdom holds Kennedy used the "Trollope ploy"—answering only the first, softer letter and pretending not to receive the second. But Frederick reveals the outcome actually accepted both letters' demands: the public statement said only that Soviets yielded and withdrew Cuban missiles, but Kennedy privately agreed to withdraw Turkish missiles—a secret deal never mentioned publicly.

45:11 One Soviet officer's dissenting vote blocked nuclear war
On Black Saturday, American destroyers dropped depth charges on Soviet submarine B-59. The boat's commander, Savitsky, believed World War III had begun and ordered preparation to fire a 15-kiloton nuclear torpedo at U.S. warships. Under Soviet protocol, firing required unanimous agreement from three officers aboard. Two consented; only Arkhipov dissented. The nuclear attack was never executed. Frederick argues the crisis didn't spiral into nuclear war because both Kennedy and Khrushchev possessed the capacity to think from the other side's perspective. But this incident reveals the entire process was riddled with countless contingent nodes where things could spiral out of control.

56:50 Not until 1963 did he first call civil rights a moral issue
From 1962 to '63, street conflict in the civil rights movement escalated. In the James Meredith case—his fight to enter the University of Mississippi—Kennedy was forced to deploy federal marshals to escort him to campus; the images circulated nationwide. Frederick emphasizes Kennedy previously urged civil rights leaders to "wait a little longer," walking a tightrope between Southern and Black voters. Only in June 1963, in an Oval Office address, did he first frame civil rights as a "moral issue." This shift also involved diplomatic calculus—Mississippi's images had damaged American "soft power" abroad, especially in competing for Third World support.

item.title: Zhipu's R&D spending is twice its revenue; how long can free open-source models sustain growth?
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-01-asianometry-智谱研发支出是营收两倍-靠免费开源模型换增长能撑多久/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-01-asianometry-智谱研发支出是营收两倍-靠免费开源模型换增长能撑多久/
item.description: Zhipu releases all its latest models free and open-source, but R&D spending is already twice revenue—the real question, hanging unanswered at the piece's close, is how long this business of burning cash for market attention can last.
item.content:encoded:
Zhipu releases all its latest models free and open-source, but R&D spending is already twice revenue—the real question, hanging unanswered at the piece's close, is how long this business of burning cash for market attention can last.

The complete arc from Tsinghua lab to Hong Kong IPO is rarely documented; the wild swings in valuation and the burn-cash-to-grow strategy offer real insight into how Chinese AI companies model their business.

1:02 Paper-to-product culture turned knowledge graphs into revenue
Zhipu traces back to Tsinghua's Knowledge Engineering Group, founded in 1996 and focused on knowledge graphs and information extraction. The lab's internal motto was P2P—Paper to Product—reflecting the conviction that AI required industry engagement. In 2006, KEG spun out AMiner, an academic search engine. Starting in 2015, it built commercial partnerships with Microsoft, Elsevier, Google, ExxonMobil, and IBM, generating revenue that convinced the team to incorporate AMiner as a standalone company.

5:13 GPT-3's scale forced Tsinghua to bet on building its own large models
GPT-3's release in 2020, with 175 billion parameters and generation quality far exceeding Google's BERT and other mainstream models at the time, made Zhang Peng realize that classical NLP's complex syntactic pipeline was unnecessary. His advisor Zhang Bo agreed the large language model represented a new paradigm but warned that models ‘spout utter nonsense’and don't truly understand what they say. Zhang Peng pushed ahead anyway, rallying the team to train their own billions-parameter Chinese-English bilingual model. With OpenAI's details unpublished, they had to discover everything themselves.

8:21 GLM proved that blending BERT-style fill-in-the-blank with GPT-style generation works at scale
In the WuDao project of 2021, Tsinghua proposed GLM (General Language Model), a pretraining framework that used bidirectional context to fill blanks like BERT, but generated token-by-token like GPT rather than predicting entire masked spans at once. Beyond 100 billion parameters, the model began showing signs of intent understanding—for example, on arithmetic questions about a newborn's head length, it divided rather than simply multiplying 50 by 1/4, suggesting it grasped the problem's underlying logic rather than pattern-matching formulas.

11:27 GLM-130B went open-source because monetization looked impossible at the time
In 2022, Zhipu trained GLM-130B, a 130-billion-parameter dense model (avoiding the sparse mixture-of-experts used in WuDao 2.0) chosen so it could run on a single A100 server. Training compute cost roughly 4 million yuan, with total end-to-end cost around 10 million yuan. After successful training, the team chose to open-source it—Zhang Peng's reasoning was blunt: even closed-source, it wouldn't make money anyway, so trade it for reputation. GLM-130B became the only Chinese model to appear on Stanford's November 2022 large model benchmark report.

16:47 Consumer chat lost to Baidu and ByteDance; Zhipu pivoted entirely to enterprise
Zhipu's consumer chatbot, Zhipu Qingyan, launched in August 2023 as one of China's earliest but couldn't compete against Baidu's Wenxin and ByteDance-backed Doubao. Doubao eventually reached 324 million monthly active users; Qingyan peaked below 11 million. Paid subscriptions saw no consumer appetite.
